Ibn Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri stress that the clarity of the sign obliged Pharaoh to acknowledge the truth, yet he chose the strategy of accusation. The commentators do not settle the exact nature of the hand's light.

This verse relates Pharaoh's words to the nobles surrounding him after Moses displayed his staff turned into a manifest serpent and his hand shining white. Pharaoh declared that Moses is a knowledgeable magician, meaning skilled and expert in sorcery, thereby trying to present the sign as mere magic. He then stirred his people by claiming that Moses wants to drive them out of their land through his magic, and asked them what they advise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi explain that Pharaoh aimed to frighten his people and obscure the proof, since leaving one's homeland is among the hardest things. Al-Tabari notes that the address «you» refers to the Copts, while those to be expelled were the children of Israel whom they had enslaved. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya see in the phrasing a sign of Pharaoh's bewilderment, as he now consults his subjects rather than commanding them. The commentators agree that the nobles advised postponing the matter and gathering the magicians, and some report that they suggested imprisonment, while killing Moses was not proposed because his argument was strong. Al-Razi adds that belief in sorcery was widespread at that time. Readers differ between sahhar and sahir, the former being read as an intensive form indicating a trade, whereas Ibn Atiyya regards both readings as conveying essentially the same meaning.

In this verse Pharaoh addresses the nobles around him after the sign of the staff and the hand: Moses, he says, is a very skilled magician who wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery, so what do you advise? Al-Tabari explains that the address to 'you' is to the Copts, while the real aim is the departure of the children of Israel, whom the Copts had enslaved; Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi follow this reading, and al-Sam'ani and Ibn 'Ashur confirm it by noting that the Copts had made the Israelites their servants.

The commentators generally read the speech as a political manoeuvre. Pharaoh, defeated by the proof, turns the matter into one of kingship and land. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that he aims to turn people against Moses by stirring the fear of leaving one's homeland. Al-Mawardi offers two possible reasons for the consultation: a wish to win hearts, or a bewilderment that left Pharaoh seeking counsel. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take the word 'you command' as consultation rather than order, and stress the humiliation of a self-proclaimed god asking his subjects for advice.

The nobles' reply, reported by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi, is to delay Moses and his brother and to summon every learned sorcerer. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi observe that they do not propose killing Moses, since his proof is clear and they fear unrest. Ibn 'Ashur notes that they repeat Pharaoh's own words to show full agreement. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri add that this consultation is also a means to rally the people against the prophet.

Sayyid Qutb draws a general lesson from the passage about tyrants who turn conciliatory once they feel the ground slipping beneath them. These readings are not unanimous, but they agree on the essentials: Pharaoh's speech aims to turn the people away from Moses' mission.

This verse reports what Pharaoh's chiefs advised him after Moses had shown the staff and the hand: to put off the matter of Moses and his brother Aaron and to send men into the cities of Egypt to gather every skilled magician. The commentators broadly agree that the verb means to postpone, though some, such as al-Baghawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, also allow the sense of detaining him. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi all read it this way. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya say that Pharaoh feared that killing Moses would create doubt among the people, so they advised delay while the magicians were assembled to oppose him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the reply "every skilled magician" answers Pharaoh's words "a skilled magician", to calm his anxiety. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the form "sahhar" denotes a craft or great proficiency, while Ibn 'Uthaymin prefers the sense of surpassing skill. Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn Kathir report that God arranged this gathering so that His signs would be displayed openly before people on the day of the festival. The main difference lies in the nature of the delay and in what Pharaoh intended by it.

This verse reports what Pharaoh said to the notables around him after seeing the signs of Moses' staff and hand. He called Moses a knowing magician, warned them that he wanted to drive them from their land by his magic, and asked for their counsel. They advised him to delay the matter of Moses and his brother and to send agents through the cities to gather every skilled magician. The commentators agree that the 'summoners' were officers who gathered people and magicians, and that the phrase 'every knowing magician' expresses totality and exaggeration, meant to calm Pharaoh's anxiety after he had run out of arguments. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that Pharaoh, lacking proof, turned to intimidation and arrogance, while al-Razi holds that he sought to turn his people against Moses by mentioning the pain of leaving one's homeland, and that his question 'what do you advise?' was meant to win them over.

Opinions differ on the meaning of 'arjih'. Most take it as postponement, while others take it as detention, as reported by al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. Ibn Atiyya notes that the notables did not advise killing Moses, since his proof was clear. Ibn Ashur considers that 'sahhar' is in practice the same as 'sahir', while Ibn Uthaymin holds that it is an intensive form that also carries the sense of a trade. Some readers recite 'bi-kulli sahir', as al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan report.

This verse tells that Pharaoh had the magicians gathered for an appointed time, a known day, which the commentators identify as the Day of Adornment, a festival, at the time of mid-morning. Ibn Abbas reported that this day fell on a Saturday at the beginning of the year, the day of Nowruz. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi agree that the appointed time was the forenoon of that day, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Zayd state that the gathering took place in Alexandria. The commentators agree that the purpose of the assembly was to make the magicians' victory visible before the people. Al-Razi explains that Pharaoh, blinded by his love of power, accepted the advice of his courtiers and wanted the contest to take place before a large crowd, which Moses himself also wanted so that his proof would be seen by all. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur explain that the call to the people was a way of urging them to attend, and that the words about following the magicians meant remaining loyal to Pharaoh's religion rather than literally following the magicians. Ibn Ashur adds that the conditional form shows the magicians did not doubt their victory. These commentaries present the verse as a public display whose meaning the scholars read in different ways.

The verse reports that Pharaoh had the magicians gathered for an appointed day, the Day of Adornment, and that the people were called to attend the contest. The commentators generally read the question "Will you gather?" as a call urging the people to hurry and assemble, a rhetorical question meant as an order and an encouragement. The people's words "that we may follow the magicians" are understood by most to mean that they would follow the magicians in their religion and abandon Moses. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that "la'alla" here means "so that", and that the real aim is not to follow Moses; al-Zamakhshari calls this a metonymy. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that some took the words as mockery, the magicians being in their sense Moses and Aaron and their people. Ibn Kathir observes that the people followed their king's religion without seeking the truth. Ibn al-Jawzi mentions that the day was a festival of the Egyptians, while Ibn Zayd placed the gathering in Alexandria, and Ibn 'Abbas linked the day to Nawruz. Ibn 'Uthaymin sees partisanship in the phrasing, though he notes a degree of fairness in the conditional clause "if they are the victors".

This passage describes how Pharaoh gathered the magicians for an appointed day, the day of the festival, and called the people to assemble and watch the contest. The people's words, "perhaps we shall follow the magicians if they are the victors," mean for most commentators that they hoped to remain on their own religion and not follow Moses, so the phrase is an indirect expression rather than a real intention to follow magic. Al-Tabari holds that the particle here means "so that," a reading also adopted by Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the phrase as an indirect expression of the same aim, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a way of rejecting Moses. Ibn Kathir stresses that the people followed their king's religion rather than the truth itself. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi stress the urgent sense of the question, with the speakers urging the crowd to assemble. Ibn Zayd places the gathering in Alexandria, while most other commentators do not specify a location. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that the phrasing betrays partisanship, since they should have said "we shall follow the victor." The commentators therefore agree on the general sense, while differing on the grammatical function of the particle, on how the interrogation should be read, and on the place of the gathering.

This verse reports that the magicians, gathered by Pharaoh to confront Moses, asked for a reward if they should prevail, and Pharaoh agreed and added the promise that they would be among his close companions. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the reward as wealth and the status they would gain with the king, and the nearness as rank and influence at court. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the question carries the sense of a conditional, which accounts for the placement of the word idhan. Ibn 'Ashur sees the request as a way of securing Pharaoh's promise before they begin, since they knew how badly he needed them. Commentators note several readings of the interrogative and of the word for yes, none of which alters the meaning. For the preceding phrase, 'perhaps we may follow the magicians', most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, take it to mean Pharaoh's magicians, whereas Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as following them in defending their religion rather than learning magic, and some hold it was said mockingly of Moses and Aaron. Ibn Kathir notes that the magicians' number varies among reports. Al-Razi observes that Pharaoh, blinded by his pride, accepted their suggestion so the debate would take place before a vast crowd.

This verse records Pharaoh's answer to the magicians who, having come to his court, asked for a reward if they won against Moses. He agreed and added that they would be among those brought near to him. The commentators agree on the core meaning: Pharaoh promised them both wealth and high rank. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud explain that 'idhan' here introduces the conditional response to their request, and that 'na'am' restates the question; the reading 'ni'im' with a kasra is noted as an equivalent variant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir observe that the magicians asked for pay on condition of victory, and that they sought to follow their king's religion rather than the truth. Ibn Juzayy clarifies that following the magicians meant supporting their faith, not practising magic, since magic was forbidden. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the gathering took place in Egypt, while Ibn Zayd places it in Alexandria. Al-Tabari, following Ibn Zayd, reads 'la'alla' as meaning 'so that'. Al-Razi sees the day of the festival as chosen so that Moses' proof would be witnessed by a large crowd. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress Pharaoh's political calculation in offering rewards to secure allies. The commentators do not settle between the readings, but agree on the import of the promise.

The commentators explain that Moses, after the magicians offered either to throw first or to let him throw first, said to them: Throw what you are going to throw, meaning your ropes and staffs. Most of them agree that this is not a command to practise magic but a permission to let them do first what they were going to do anyway, so that the truth would then appear and falsehood be exposed. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi stress that Moses neither ordered sorcery nor approved deception. Al-Razi adds other readings, such as a threat or a conditional sense: if you are in the right. Ibn Kathir reports that the magicians then threw their ropes and staffs, swearing by the might of Pharaoh that they would win, and that God made Moses' staff rise up and swallow what they had fabricated. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the oath by Pharaoh's might in two ways, either as a real oath or as an invocation of blessing. Ibn 'Atiyya leaves both readings open. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the magicians then fell down in prostration after recognising the truth, and that Pharaoh threatened them, but they replied that they feared nothing. Overall, the commentators agree on the sense: Moses lets his opponents show what they can do so that the truth may then shine forth.

This verse describes the moment when Pharaoh's magicians, gathered for the day of festivity, throw their ropes and staffs before Moses and swear by the might of Pharaoh that they will be the victors. The commentators explain that this kind of oath belonged to pre-Islamic custom, and that the 'might of Pharaoh' refers to his strength and authority. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that swearing by anything other than God is not valid in Islam. Al-Tabari reads the preposition as an oath and says the magicians swore by Pharaoh's power, his dominion and the strength of his kingdom. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan offer another reading, in which the preposition expresses blessing and exaltation, as when a believer begins with the name of God, since these people worshipped Pharaoh. Al-Razi explains that the magicians displayed a confidence close to certainty, which afterwards strengthened the case for Moses.

The commentators agree that the ropes and staffs were very numerous, and that the magicians had been brought from various cities of Egypt. Ibn Kathir reports very different estimates of their number, from twelve thousand to eighty thousand, without choosing among them. Al-Razi notes disagreement about the number of ropes and staffs and holds that the Quran indicates they were many. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the account is condensed here, since the focus lies on what follows the casting.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Qasimi and al-Baydawi relate that their assurance came from confidence in themselves and their skill in magic, and that their oath expressed their pride.

This verse describes the decisive moment of the contest between Moses and the magicians: Moses threw down his staff, and it swallowed up what the magicians had faked by their deception, namely the ropes and staffs they had made appear to be slithering snakes. The commentators agree that the staff engulfed everything the magicians had brought, and that the magicians then realized what they were witnessing was not sorcery, so they fell down prostrate in belief. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the swallowing was a real event, while others regard the magic as illusion that vanishes before the truth. Opinions differ on who caused the magicians to fall in the phrase 'the magicians were cast down prostrate': al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that God was the agent by placing decisive conviction in their hearts, whereas others take the verb to simply mean 'to fall' and see no need to supply an agent. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi report that these men, masters of their craft, recognized that the sign exceeded magic and passed in an instant from disbelief to faith, becoming martyrs. On recitation, Hafs reads 'talqafu' with a single taa and a light qaf, while most readers read 'talaqqafu' with a doubled taa, which Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi explain as the dropping of one of the two taas.

This verse describes the moment the magicians, having seen Moses' staff swallow what they had produced, fall prostrate before God as though something had seized and cast them down. The commentators agree that this prostration came from their certainty that the sign was not magic and lay beyond human power, and they declared their faith in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress the speed and sincerity of this turn, while al-Zamakhshari explains that the verb "was cast" means simply "fell down", chosen to match the throwing verbs before it. On who did the casting, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi attribute it to God who guided them, though al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari consider it better not to name any agent; Abu Hayyan objects that a passive verb needs a stated subject. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur report that Pharaoh threatened the magicians with having their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides and crucifixion, and that they replied there was no harm to them, since they would return to their Lord. The commentators differ on the number of magicians, which Ibn Kathir reports in widely varying figures, God alone knowing the true count. For these scholars the episode stands as a clear proof of the truth of Moses' message before the assembled people.

This verse reports the words of the magicians after Moses' staff swallowed what they had made of ropes and staffs: they fell down prostrate and said, we believe in the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Lord of the worlds is the God to whom Moses called, not Pharaoh. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi see the phrase Lord of Moses and Aaron as an explanatory apposition that removes any confusion with Pharaoh, who claimed lordship, and that points to the sign God performed through these two prophets as the reason for their faith. The commentators agree that the conversion was sudden and rested on the conviction that the miracle lay beyond the reach of magic. Al-Razi notes that their expertise in sorcery allowed them to recognise this. Ibn Kathir observes that truth prevails whenever it confronts falsehood. Al-Sha'rawi and others regard the prostration as almost involuntary, so strong was the evidence. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that Pharaoh threatened to cut off their hands and feet and crucify them, and they replied that this would not harm them, since they would return to their Lord. Opinions differ on the number of magicians and their later fate, and no commentator settles the question. On grammar, Abu Hayyan debates whether the passive verb cast down implies a hidden agent, while al-Zamakhshari suggested that none need be supposed.

The commentators explain that this verse records the faith of the magicians after Moses' staff swallowed what they had made to look like serpents. They fell down in prostration and said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds," then specified, "the Lord of Moses and Aaron," to show that this Lord is the one who sent these two prophets and worked the miracle through them, not Pharaoh who claimed lordship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present this sense, while al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a clarification that removes any confusion with Pharaoh's claim; al-Nasafi adds that Pharaoh, hearing "Lord of the worlds," thought the phrase referred to himself, which is why the specification was added. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the magicians believed at the moment they recognised that the feat exceeded human power. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi draw from the account that magic's limit is the deception of the senses, and that deep knowledge of the craft enables one to recognise the truth. The commentators do not agree on the number of magicians: Ibn Kathir cites widely varying figures without settling the matter. Ibn 'Ashur, al-Jaza'iri and others stress that Pharaoh's threats did not shake their faith. Al-Qurtubi reports the debate of al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and others over the meaning of "the first of the believers." Modern works such as Sayyid Qutb's emphasise the sudden turn of the magicians from hired men to believers.

This passage tells how the magicians, seeing the sign of the staff swallowing what they had faked, recognised that it came from God and not from sorcery. They fell prostrate and declared: we believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh rebuked them for believing without his permission, claimed that Moses was their great master who had taught them magic, and threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them all. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that Pharaoh aimed to confuse his people so they would not think the magicians had believed with insight, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi read it as an attempt to discredit Moses. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, however, judge the accusation plainly absurd, since the magicians had never met Moses before. The magicians replied, no harm: they would suffer nothing from worldly torment because they would return to their Lord. Al-Razi sees in this answer a pure faith that seeks only God's pleasure. Commentators differ on the meaning of their hope for forgiveness: al-Razi allows that it may express certainty or mere supposition. Al-Farra' takes it as the first believers of their own time, a view al-Zajjaj rejects because the Children of Israel had believed before them, so the meaning becomes the first believers among the Copts or among those present. The reading with kasra in the phrase in kunna is treated by al-Farra' and the Kufans as a condition whose truth is assured. Reports about the number of magicians and of Moses' followers vary, and the commentators do not settle the matter.

The commentators explain that the sorcerers, having believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron, were threatened by Pharaoh with the cutting of their hands and feet on opposite sides and with crucifixion. They answered that there was no harm to them, for they would return to their Lord, who would reward their patience. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd take the word dayr to mean harm, and Al-Tabari says they were patient under Pharaoh's punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the punishment of this world is brief and that death by killing is the lightest and most hoped-for of the causes of death. Al-Razi adds that their words show they sought nearness to God, not only reward or fear of punishment. All agree that their hope for forgiveness of their sins is a request for pardon. They differ on the meaning of 'the first of the believers': al-Tabari and al-Baydawi take it to mean the first among Pharaoh's followers or among those present at the scene, while al-Farra' says it means the first believers of their own time, a view al-Zajjaj rejects since the Children of Israel had already believed. Al-Qurtubi notes that the reading with a kasra on inna, held by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, forms a conditional, which al-Zamakhshari explains by the example of a worker who claims his wage. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the expression of hope is a form of courtesy towards God, who does as He wills.

This passage reports the reply of the magicians to Pharaoh, who had threatened to cut off their hands and feet and crucify them: no harm can come to us, for we shall return to our Lord, and we hope that He will forgive our past sins, because we are the first of the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand this as the first believers among Pharaoh's people or in their own time, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it to mean the first believers among Pharaoh's followers or among those present at that gathering. Al-Farra' reads it as the first believers of their age, but al-Zajjaj rejects this, since the Children of Israel had believed before them. Al-Zamakhshari explains that "no harm" means no injury, and that patience under the threat erases sins and earns reward; al-Razi sees in their words "we shall return to our Lord" a sign that they believed out of longing for God's pleasure alone, seeking neither reward nor fearing punishment. Most commentators take the word "tat'amu" as hope, though al-Razi allows that it may mean certainty, as in Abraham's words. The reading "in kunna" with a kasra is explained by al-Zamakhshari as a conditional used by one who is certain of his standing, and by others as an expression of self-abasement. The commentators also note that Pharaoh's threat only strengthened their faith. The context is Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel and Pharaoh's pursuit, as recorded by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir.

God relates that He revealed to Moses to set out by night with His servants, the Children of Israel, because Pharaoh and his armies would pursue them; this stated reason is the core meaning of the verse, as the commentators note. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the "servants" are the Children of Israel, that to "set out by night" means to travel at night, and that the aim was to get ahead of Pharaoh and reach the sea before he caught up with them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the night departure was meant to put them ahead so that Pharaoh would follow them into the sea, which would then close over him. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report that this revelation came after Moses had spent years among his people calling them with signs and finding only persistence in defiance, and that it marked the point at which victory was assured. Most exegetes mention that the Children of Israel borrowed jewellery from the Copts before leaving, and the account of Moses seeking the tomb of Joseph, which an old woman showed him; these reports, given with chains of transmission some scholars consider weak, are presented as such. The size of the forces divides the commentators sharply: Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Suddi speak of six hundred thousand fighting men among the Children of Israel, but al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir draw no firm conclusion from this. The exegetes do not settle between these views; what the verse establishes is that Moses left with a great multitude and that Pharaoh followed with forces far greater in number. The tafsirs conclude that the command to depart by night served God's purpose of deliverance for the believers and destruction for the disbelievers.

This verse describes Pharaoh's reaction when he learned that the Children of Israel had set out by night: he sent men into the cities of his realm to gather the people and muster the army to pursue them. The commentators report that he told his people these were only a small band, although they had angered him by opposing his religion, killing the Egyptian firstborn, taking the borrowed ornaments and leaving his land without permission. He also declared that he and his people were wary and ready. The exegetes agree that shirdhima means a small group or the base remnant of something, and that the smallness described may refer to number or to weakness and low standing. They also agree that hashirin means gathering the soldiers and the guards. On the number of the Children of Israel, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir cite six hundred thousand and seventy thousand, while al-Alusi and al-Shawkani regard these reports as confused and hold that Pharaoh's army was far larger. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the call to vigilance a principle of political caution. On the readings hadhirun, hadhirun and hadirun, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj distinguish between the one who is alert and the one who is armed, while others regard the forms as two words with the same meaning. The commentators do not settle the matter, and al-Tabari considers the readings equally well transmitted.

This verse records Pharaoh's words to his commanders when he learns that the Children of Israel have left by night with Moses. He sends agents to the cities of Egypt to gather the army, then declares that these people are a small, contemptible band who enrage him by rejecting his religion, killing his first-born, carrying off the borrowed jewelry and leaving his land without permission, and that he and his people are alert and ready to pursue them. The commentators agree that "shirdhima" means a small group or remnant. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi report, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, a number of about six hundred thousand, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi judge that the smallness is relative to Pharaoh's forces, and Ibn Uthaymin considers these figures unfounded. On "ghaziun", al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi mention several readings: the killing of the first-born, the loss of the borrowed goods, or the forced departure. On "hadhirun" and "hadhirun", al-Tabari, al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir explain that these are close forms, one meaning armed and prepared, the other watchful. Al-Razi links these variants to subtle differences in habit or disposition. Most exegetes see Pharaoh's words as serving both to encourage his troops and to reassure his people.

This verse records Pharaoh's words to his agents in the cities: the Children of Israel are a small band, they provoke him greatly, and he and his people are fully alert and prepared against them. The commentators explain that "shirdhima" means a small group, and that Pharaoh uses this description to belittle them, even though the reports cited by al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir put their number at six hundred thousand, while Pharaoh's army was far larger. As for what angered him, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi mention several explanations: the killing of the Egyptians' firstborn, the taking away of borrowed jewellery and goods, or their departure without permission. Al-Tabari considers all of these possible. Al-Razi adds their religious difference and their refusal to treat Pharaoh as a god. On the word "hadhirun", the readings differ: the majority reading means watchful, while the Kufan reading "hadhirun" means equipped and ready. Al-Tabari and most exegetes consider the two readings close in meaning. Al-Razi distinguishes the adjective, which expresses a lasting quality, from the active participle, which expresses a renewed state. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the statement a call to political caution, while Ibn 'Uthaymin combines vigilance and readiness in the sense of both readings.

The Qur'an reports that Pharaoh, having learned that Moses had led the Children of Israel out by night, sent men to the cities of Egypt to gather the troops to pursue them. He told his people that these are only a small band, that they had provoked him by opposing his religion, killing the firstborn of the Copts, taking away the jewelry they had borrowed, and leaving his land without permission, and that he and his people are alert and ready for them. The commentators read these words as a call to mobilize and as a way to reassure the population. As for the size of this 'small band', at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit, from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others, about six hundred thousand men, while al-Mawardi lists several different estimates. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the word 'small' describes their weakness relative to Pharaoh's vast army, or their lowly status, rather than their number.

The reading of the last word is disputed. 'Hadhirun' is the reading of Medina and Abu 'Amr, 'hadhirun' with an alif is that of the Kufans and Ibn 'Amir, and 'hadirun' with an undotted dal is a rare reading. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i distinguish the hadhir, one whose caution is part of his nature, from the hadhir, one who is constantly on guard and prepared. Abu 'Ubayda and Sibawayh see the two forms as having the same meaning. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas explain the sense as 'equipped and armed', an interpretation adopted by an-Nahhas and Ibn 'Atiyya.

The commentators agree that the verse shows Pharaoh's excessive caution and his wish to appear in full control. Some, such as al-Baghawi, note that these words also served to justify the mobilization before the people of the cities.

The commentators explain that this verse describes God expelling Pharaoh and his people from the gardens along the Nile, its flowing springs, their treasures and their noble dwelling, meaning that God stripped them of these blessings before their destruction. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the "gardens" were orchards on both banks of the Nile and the "springs" were its flowing waters or canals. Mujahid explained that the treasures were so called because none of their wealth had been spent in obedience to God, while others took them to be buried riches. The "noble station" was read by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid as pulpits, by others as the assemblies of notables or fine dwellings, and al-Mawardi also mentions stables for horses. The commentators agree that the pronoun in "We expelled them" refers to Pharaoh and his people, and that "thus did We bequeath them to the Children of Israel" means these possessions passed to the Israelites after the drowning. They differ on how far this inheritance went: al-Hasan holds that the Israelites returned to Egypt, whereas Ibn Ashur argues they never ruled Egypt and that the meaning concerns comparable blessings given in Syria. As for "they pursued them at sunrise", most take it to mean the moment the sun was rising, while Abu Ubayda understands it as heading eastward.

This verse describes what befell Pharaoh and his people after they pursued the Children of Israel. God removed them from gardens, springs, treasures and a noble station, meaning He stripped them of the blessings they had enjoyed. Commentators differ on the noble station: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it to mean pulpits, al-Mawardi and others understand the assemblies of rulers and notables surrounded by their followers, al-Naqqash says fine dwellings, and Ibn Lahi'a identifies it with al-Fayyoum. Regarding the treasures, Mujahid explains they were so called because their owners never spent from them in obedience to God, al-Dahhak takes them to be rivers, while most understand stores or buried wealth. On the word 'kadhalika' (thus), al-Tabari and others read it as referring to the manner just described, al-Zamakhshari lists three grammatical possibilities, and Ibn 'Ashur treats it as a parenthetical remark. All agree that God gave these blessings to the Children of Israel, yet al-Hasan holds that they returned to Egypt, while al-Tabari holds that their dwellings were in Syria, and Ibn 'Ashur denies any lasting Israelite rule over Egypt. Finally, for 'mushriqin', most read it as entering the time of sunrise, whereas Abu 'Ubayda takes it as heading east.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the account of the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. The word "thus" refers to the expulsion just described: God removed Pharaoh's people from their gardens, springs, treasures and noble station, and then gave all of it as an inheritance to the Children of Israel. Most agree that the gardens and springs are the orchards and waterways on both banks of the Nile in Egypt, and that the "noble station" means fine dwellings or pleasant assemblies. They differ on its meaning: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to be pulpits, Ibn Jubayr to be fine residences, and others to be the councils of rulers. Mujahid explains that the wealth is called treasure because it was never spent in obedience to God, while al-Dahhak takes the treasures to be rivers.

The meaning of inheritance is disputed. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after Pharaoh drowned and took their homes and property, a view also reported by al-Sam'ani. Ibn Atiyya allows that the inheritance may refer to Syria or, after a long time, to Egypt. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Juzayy argue that history does not show Israelite rule over Egypt afterwards, so they read the inheritance as a gift elsewhere; al-Shawkani and Ibn Uthaymin understand it as a divine bestowal, and al-Sha'rawi recalls the promise of a similar land in Syria.

On "fa-atba'uhum mushriqin", most take it as Pharaoh's army overtaking them at sunrise, while Abu Ubayda reads it as heading towards the east. Some explain the delay by the burial of the firstborn of Pharaoh's people.

This verse describes what happened to Pharaoh and his people after God's judgement: He drove them out of their gardens, springs, treasures and noble station, and then gave all of it as an inheritance to the Children of Israel. As for the phrase "they followed them at sunrise", the commentators agree that it means Pharaoh and his army caught up with the Children of Israel at the time of sunrise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the gardens, springs and treasures refer to the wealth the Egyptians held along the Nile, and most report that the "noble station" means raised platforms, assemblies or fine dwellings. Al-Zamakhshari discusses several ways of parsing the word "thus" in the sentence. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the inheritance means the Children of Israel received things that had not been theirs, without implying that they recovered the land of Egypt itself. Al-Qurtubi reports that the inheritance may refer to a return to Egypt, or to the ornaments they had borrowed from the Copts. Some commentators say Pharaoh's delay was due either to the death of the firstborn among his people or to a cloud that covered them until morning. The exegetes do not settle these details and report the views as they were transmitted.

When the two hosts came in sight of each other, the companions of Moses said, "We are surely going to be overtaken." The commentators explain that they had the sea in front of them and Pharaoh's army behind them, and that their fear came from this apparently hopeless position. Moses replied with "No!" (kalla), meaning they would not be overtaken, because his Lord was with him and would guide him to safety. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take "He will guide me" as guidance to a way of escape, while as-Suddi and al-Mawardi read it as "He will suffice me." The verb "came in sight" means each side saw the other. Some readers used the doubled form "mudarrakun", and az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take it to mean being destroyed one after another, although they do not settle the question. God then ordered Moses to strike the sea with his staff, and it split into twelve paths, one for each tribe, each part like a towering mountain. God brought Pharaoh and his people near, and then drowned them. Ibn Kathir adds that the ground between the paths was dry. The commentators report many traditions about the details of the miracle, but they do not draw a firm conclusion from them.

Moses answered his people, who saw Pharaoh and his army drawing near while the sea lay before them: No, never! My Lord is with me, and He will guide me. The commentators agree that Moses, fully trusting God's promise, dispels his people's fear; that the word "kalla" is a rejection and a warning against thinking they will be overtaken; and that the divine presence here means help and protection. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "sayahdini" means He will show him the way to salvation. Al-Suddi, as transmitted by al-Tabari and al-Mawardi, gives a different reading: God will suffice him against them. Al-Razi sees two successive assurances, protection and guidance. Nearly all link the passage to the miracle of the parting of the sea: Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that Joshua asked where God had commanded them to go, and Moses replied "here," which showed the command was divine. Accounts of the number of Pharaoh's soldiers or of the Israelites differ widely among authors, and several exegetes admit they cannot be treated as certain. Variant readings of the word "mudrakun" concern mainly the vocalisation and do not change the basic idea of being overtaken or destroyed.

This passage from Surat al-Shu'ara' recounts the miracle of the sea splitting for Moses. God commanded him to strike the sea with his staff; it parted, and each section became like a mighty mountain. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, agree that the parting was for the Children of Israel, that the sea became twelve paths corresponding to the twelve tribes, each tribe having its own, and that God made dry ground for them. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that the water rose on both sides of the path until it resembled mountains, and that God made openings through which they could see one another when they feared for their companions.

The commentators stress that the event was accomplished by God's power, the striking of the staff being only an apparent means. They differ on which sea is meant: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir identify it with the Red Sea, while a view reported by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, and attributed to al-Naqqash, identifies it with the Nile. As for the number of Pharaoh's army and of the Children of Israel, the reports are numerous and divergent; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi consider them to belong to the Israelite narratives and not to be relied upon.

All agree that the word "tawd" means a great mountain, and al-Tabari and al-Razi cite verses of early poets to illustrate it. On the phrase "wa-azlafna thumma al-akharin", al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean that God brought Pharaoh and his people near the sea, while Abu 'Ubayda understands it as gathering them together, and al-Zajjaj judges both meanings acceptable.

The commentators explain that this verse describes what happened at the sea when Pharaoh and his army drew close to the Children of Israel. God brought Pharaoh's people near the water until they entered the paths that had opened in the sea, and then the water closed over them, while Moses and those with him were saved. The commentators differ on the meaning of the verb azlafna. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean bringing near: God brought Pharaoh and his people close. Abu Ubayda understands it as gathering together, meaning that they were brought together into the sea so that none of them would escape. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the bringing near may be toward the Children of Israel or toward the sea, and he mentions the reading azlaqna with a qaf, meaning that their feet were made to slip or their power was removed. Al-Razi also considers that a cloud may have held them back.

The commentators agree that the others are Pharaoh's people, that Moses and his followers were saved while their opponents drowned, that this was a sign and a lesson, and that most of the Prophet's people would not believe. God is described as mighty in retribution and merciful to His allies. Ibn Ashur explains that they were emboldened to the point of entering the paths they saw the Children of Israel using.

Some exegetes relate details about Gabriel who guided the Children of Israel and drove back the Copts, or about Pharaoh's words as he drowned, but Ibn Kathir and others do not vouch for the authenticity of these accounts. God knows the full details of these events.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the rescue of Moses and all who were with him, including the Children of Israel, after the sea parted for them into dry paths, and then closed over Pharaoh and his people, who were drowned. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect the verse to what precedes it: God brought Pharaoh and his troops close to the sea, and the "others" are Pharaoh's people. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take "azlafna" to mean "brought near," while Abu Ubayda, followed by al-Zajjaj, takes it to mean "gathered together"; al-Zajjaj considers both acceptable, since gathering them brings them close to one another. Some readers recited "azlaqna" with a qaf, meaning to make them slip, or to bring down their power, according to al-Zamakhshari.

The commentators agree that the rescue came from the sea being held in its parted state until Moses and his people had crossed, and that the drowning came when the sea closed over the pursuers who had entered after them. Al-Razi lists several miraculous aspects of the event, and al-Tabari reports the role of Gabriel urging on Pharaoh's mount. Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabari see in the verse a sign and a lesson, and note that most people did not believe, which serves as consolation for the Prophet. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir mention that few Egyptians believed, such as Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, while others extend this to the wider population of Egypt.

The differences concern mainly details: Ibn Atiyya raises the possibility that the sea was the Nile, while al-Alusi and others identify it with the Red Sea. The verse ends by affirming that God is mighty in His vengeance against His enemies and merciful toward His believers.

The commentators explain that the words "Then We drowned the others" mean that God destroyed Pharaoh and his people by closing the sea over them after they had entered it in pursuit of Moses and the Children of Israel, who had already crossed safely to the other shore. The verse thus belongs to the account of the parting of the sea and marks the completion of the destruction of the wrongdoers. Ibn Kathir and others report that the sea closed over them once they had all entered, so that none escaped. Scholars agree that the drowning came by the waters closing over them, and that the verse draws attention to the greatness of the sign and its lesson. Nearly all identify "the others" as Pharaoh and his people, though their phrasing of the context varies.

The views differ, however, on what preceded the drowning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that Gabriel drove the Children of Israel forward and stood between the two camps, and that Pharaoh hesitated at the sea before entering it when his horsemen followed a mare that drew them on. They also cite the report that God commanded the sea to close, and the report that Pharaoh declared his faith at the point of drowning, a declaration that was rebuked. Ibn 'Atiyya mentions that the sea closed after Moses had reached the far bank, without settling the details. Al-Qurtubi notes that the numbers of Pharaoh's army and of the Children of Israel are transmitted in varying forms, and none can be held as certain.

Al-Razi dwells on the verse as a sign of miraculous power, and sees in it a consolation for the Prophet, reminding him that most people do not believe even in the face of miracles. Ibn 'Ashur adds that Pharaoh's crossing preceded the closing of the sea over him once he was in its midst.

The commentators explain that the verse refers to what God did to Pharaoh and his people, drowning them in the sea after saving Moses and his followers. It is a clear sign and a lesson about God's power and the truthfulness of His messenger. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir agree that the "others" are Pharaoh's people. The majority who did not believe are the Egyptians of the Copts who remained in disbelief. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that only a few believed: Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, the believer from Pharaoh's family, and the old woman who showed Moses the tomb of Joseph, while Muqatil also names Maryam, daughter of Nasmusa. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur see the verse as a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to his people, since most people did not believe despite the striking signs. Ibn Ashur holds that the reference covers the whole story. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi recall that the Children of Israel themselves worshipped the calf and asked to see God, so they too were not mostly believers. Abu al-Su'ud favours a return of the pronoun to the Prophet's own people and objects to referring it to Pharaoh's people. Ibn 'Uthaymin accepts both readings and cites the final verse of the surah. Overall, the verse affirms that signs alone do not guide those whose hearts refuse them.

This passage concludes the story of Moses with Pharaoh and his people. The commentators explain that God brought Pharaoh's people near the sea until they followed the Children of Israel, then saved Moses and those with him and drowned the others. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, citing Ibn Abbas and Qatada, take the verb azlafna here to mean

God commands His Prophet to recite to the idolaters the story of Abraham, when he asked his father and people what they worshipped. They replied that they worshipped idols and remained devoted to them. He asked whether the idols heard their call, or could benefit or harm them; they had to admit they could do none of this, and justified their practice by saying they had found their fathers doing the same. The commentators agree that Abraham knew well that they were idolaters, and that his question aimed to show that what they worshipped did not deserve worship; their answer was made in pride and delight in their worship. Ibn Kathir and others explain that their words "we remain" (fa-nazallu) mean they persisted in this devotion, while al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi report that some understood it as worship performed only by day, the night being given to other stars, a view which al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi do not adopt, taking the verb to indicate continuity. On "or harm", al-Tabari sees it as the threat of confiscation or punishment against whoever abandons the cult, while Ibn al-Jawzi reads it as a threat against those who do not worship them. On "they are an enemy to me", Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi report that the idols will be hostile to their worshippers on the Day of Resurrection, al-Farra' reading it as an inversion in which Abraham is the one opposed to them, and al-Zamakhshari stressing that the statement shows his rejection of them. The exception "except the Lord of the worlds" is taken by some as continuous, since the ancestors may have worshipped God alongside their idols, and by others as discontinuous. The general meaning retained is that blind imitation of ancestors is no proof, and that only the Lord of the worlds deserves worship.

God commands His Prophet to recite to his people the story of Abraham, when he asked his father and his people what they worshipped. Abraham knew they worshipped idols, but he wanted to show them that what they worshipped deserved no worship at all. They answered that they worshipped idols and remained devoted to them. Al-Tabari explains that the word 'ukūf' here means serving them, and he reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means prayer directed to them. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Razi hold that the added phrase 'we remain devoted to them' expresses their pride and delight in this worship, while some scholars say they used 'nazullu' because they worshipped the idols only by day and not by night.

Abraham then asked whether the idols heard their prayers, or could benefit or harm them. They conceded that they could do none of this, and fell back on the example of their fathers. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Razi regard this blind imitation as among the worst forms of imitation, and note that Abraham declared his disavowal of all they worshipped except the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari takes the exception to be disconnected, whereas Ibn ʿAtiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi note that it could be connected, since some of their ancestors had worshipped God.

The commentators observe that Abraham then listed the attributes of the Lord who deserves worship: He who created me guides me, who feeds and gives me drink, who heals me when I am ill, who causes me to die and then to live again, and from whom I hope for forgiveness on the Day of Judgment. This is an argument addressed to his people: only one who does these things deserves to be worshipped.

The verse reports that Abraham asked his father and his people what they worship, and they answered that they worship idols and remain devoted to them. The commentators explain that "we remain devoted" means they persist in this worship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite Ibn Abbas that devotion here means prayer directed to the idols, and al-Qurtubi notes that some said they worshipped them only by day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that the people added the words "we remain devoted" to show their pride and delight in worshipping idols, even though the question did not require it. All agree that Abraham knew they were idol worshippers and asked only to make them see that what they worship does not deserve worship.

Abraham then asks whether the idols hear their prayers or benefit or harm them. They do not answer directly, and fall back on imitating their forefathers. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi consider this appeal to tradition the weakest kind of argument, since it offers no proof. Abraham then declares his enmity toward these objects. Al-Razi gives several explanations: the idols will become enemies of their worshippers on the Day of Judgment, or the sentence is a figure of speech. The scholars also differ on the exception "except the Lord of the worlds": al-Zamakhshari and most grammarians take it as disconnected, meaning "but the Lord of the worlds", while others, including al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, read it as connected to the ancestors who also worshipped God.

God tells His Messenger to recite to his people the story of Abraham, who asked them what they worshipped. They answered that they worshipped idols and remained devoted to them. He then asked: Do they hear you when you call upon them, or do they benefit or harm you? The commentators explain the apparent meaning as whether they hear your supplication. Qatada read it as "yusmi'unakum", meaning they make you hear an answer. The use of the present tense with "idh" evokes a past situation to make the rebuke more forceful. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the question is meant to establish the truth and silence the idolaters.

The commentators agree that the verse proves that what cannot hear, benefit or harm does not deserve worship, and that it condemns blind imitation of forefathers. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the idolaters thereby acknowledge the powerlessness of their idols. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi observe that "ta'budun" means worship, and that "sanam" is an image in human form, whether of stone or wood.

The disagreements concern mainly linguistic points. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi debate the enmity attributed to the idols in "'aduwwun li": some take it as hostility on the Day of Resurrection, others as a reversal meaning "I am their enemy". Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy discuss the omitted object in "yasma'unakum". Ibn 'Ashur explains that the dialogue leads the listeners to define for themselves the nature of their worship.

This passage recounts Abraham's exchange with his father and his people when he asked them what they worship. They answered that they worship idols and remain devoted to them. Abraham then asked whether these idols hear them when they call upon them, and whether they can benefit them if they worship them or harm them if they abandon them. Al-Tabari explains "or harm you" as meaning that the idols would punish those who stop worshipping them by taking away their wealth or destroying them. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi report that the benefit meant is provision, while the harm is what befalls one who abandons their worship. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Jalalayn and al-Nasafi link benefit to their worship and harm to its abandonment, whereas al-Baydawi holds that the harm falls on whoever turns away from them, and al-Alusi allows both readings. The people's reply is, in the view of all, a blind imitation of their forefathers: "We found our fathers doing so," which shows they had no proof beyond tradition. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the present-tense verb with "idh" evokes the past situation to confound them more effectively. Grammarians debate the implied object: some supply "hear your call," others "hear you," and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that Qatada's reading, "make you hear," means to answer. Most commentators conclude that this reasoning demonstrates the folly of worshipping what neither hears, benefits nor harms, and that religion is established by proof rather than by imitation.

This verse reports the answer of Abraham's people when he asked whether their idols heard their calls, benefited them or harmed them. They set these questions aside and said that they found their fathers doing so, and so they followed them. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: these idols hear nothing and bring neither benefit nor harm, and these people had no support except imitation of their ancestors. Al-Tabari explains that the reply turns from denial to an appeal to the practice of the fathers, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the verse as a rejection of blind imitation in religion. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that Abraham meant to establish the proof against them, and that their answer shows they could not defend their gods by reason. Ibn 'Ashur holds that they took pride in the custom of their forebears and saw the idols as symbols of the stars. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi note that scholars drew from the verse the prohibition of imitation in the foundations of belief. Al-Qurtubi reports Abraham's words that the idols are an enemy to him, which al-Farra' reads as an inversion meaning that he is their enemy. All these commentaries conclude that worship is due only to the Lord of the worlds.

God recounts how Abraham asked his father and people what they worshipped. They answered that they worshipped idols and remained devoted to them. He showed them that these idols cannot hear, benefit or harm, and they had no argument left but imitating their fathers. He then said: Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers? They are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the Worlds. The commentators largely agree on the meaning: the idols will disown their worshippers on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the word enemy means they would become enemies if worshipped on that day, citing the verse: They will deny their worship and be opposed to them. Al-Zamakhshari holds that Abraham framed the matter in terms of himself to be more persuasive, while al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba speak of an inversion: I am their enemy. On the exception, most grammarians, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya take it as disconnected, meaning but the Lord of the Worlds is my ally; Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj take it as connected, since some ancestors worshipped God alongside their idols. Abraham then describes his Lord as the one who created and guides him, who feeds and gives him drink, who heals him when he is ill, who causes him to die and then revives him, and whose forgiveness of his sin he hopes for on the Day of Judgment. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi note that he attributes illness to himself and healing to God out of courtesy towards God. Opinions differ on the sin: Mujahid and al-Hasan identify it with his words I am sick, It was the biggest of them who did it, and his remark about Sarah that she was his sister; al-Zamakhshari calls these allusions that do not require forgiveness, and al-Shawkani finds Mujahid's explanation weak.

This verse records Abraham's words to his people: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers of old? They are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds." The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the "forefathers of old" are the earlier ancestors, and that antiquity does not make falsehood true nor justify blind imitation in religion. To explain how lifeless idols can be called enemies, al-Tabari and al-Nahhas take it to mean that they will become enemies of their worshippers on the Day of Resurrection, as another verse says that they will disown their worship. Al-Farra' sees an inversion: it is Abraham who is their enemy, since whoever you oppose opposes you. Al-Zamakhshari understands the phrase as a rhetorical device: Abraham presents the matter as a personal reflection so that his advice is more readily accepted. On the exception, most grammarians consider it disconnected, meaning "but the Lord of the worlds", while al-Zajjaj and al-Tabari allow it to be connected, since some ancestors worshipped God. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi conclude that the verse condemns imitation in religion and shows that faith must rest on proof. The commentators then list the attributes of the Lord who alone deserves worship: creation, guidance, food, healing, death, resurrection and forgiveness. They explain that Abraham attributes sickness to himself and healing to God out of courtesy towards Him, and Ibn Juzayy and al-Zamakhshari note that death is ascribed to God because it is a general decree over all people.

Abraham tells his people that he disowns everything they worship, for these idols are enemies to him, except the Lord of the worlds, whom he worships alone. The commentators agree that the passage aims to refute idolatry and to show that antiquity does not make falsehood true, and that blind imitation of forefathers is no proof. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that enmity is attributed to lifeless idols because on the Day of Resurrection they will disown their worshippers. Al-Farra' holds instead that the sentence is inverted, meaning that Abraham is the enemy of the idols, since whoever you oppose also opposes you. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain the singular form by the verbal-noun pattern. On the final exception, most grammarians take it as disconnected, meaning but the Lord of the worlds, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba take it as connected, since some ancestors worshipped God. The commentators then list the attributes of the Lord: He creates, guides, feeds, gives drink, heals, causes death and gives life. They note that Abraham attributes sickness to himself and healing to God out of courtesy. As for the sin he hopes to be forgiven, some relate it to the three statements mentioned in the Quran, while others read it as the humility of the prophets.

In this verse Ibrahim describes his Lord through the blessings He bestows: the One who created him and guides him, who feeds and gives him drink, who heals him when he is sick, who causes him to die and then brings him back to life, and from whom he hopes for forgiveness on the Day of Judgment. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that these attributes serve as an argument against Ibrahim's people: the One who grants such blessings deserves to be worshipped alone, and his opponents, who acknowledge these blessings, must accept what they reject, namely resurrection and monotheism. The commentators generally understand the guidance as broad, ranging from a newborn's guidance to suckling up to guidance toward the path to Paradise, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud state. Regarding the words 'when I fall ill', most see a mark of courtesy toward God: Ibrahim attributes the illness to himself and the cure to his Lord, while he attributes death to God. Al-Zamakhshari adds that many illnesses arise from human neglect in eating and drinking. As for the 'sin' he hopes to have forgiven, Mujahid and most commentators identify it with the three lies mentioned in the Quran, which Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain as figurative speech, while others see it as a lesser fault or a failure to do what is best. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that 'hope' here expresses humble expectation of forgiveness.

In this verse Abraham states that it is God who feeds and gives him drink, making Him the sole source of his sustenance. The commentators take eating and drinking in their ordinary sense, that is, provision, and they agree that the verse lists God's favours in order to show that He alone deserves worship. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God sends the rain and brings forth fruits as provision for people, and Ibn Kathir adds that sweet water is given to people and cattle. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the mention of food and drink recalls God's grace, and that the pronoun 'He' is used to stress that He alone is the giver. Al-Sam'ani, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi report a spiritual reading in which the food is the joy of faith and the drink the sweetness of acceptance, though al-Qurtubi considers this reading far from the apparent meaning. Abu Bakr al-Warraq understands that God feeds without food or drink, and Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a reference to the continuation of life. All agree that Abraham attributes his sustenance to God out of good manners.

In this verse Abraham describes his Lord as the one who created him and guides him, who feeds and gives him drink, and who, when he falls ill, heals him. The commentators agree that healing belongs to God alone. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sickness is attributed to Abraham and the healing to God out of good manners toward the Lord, since everything comes from Him. Several scholars compare this to the words of al-Khidr, "I wished to damage it". Al-Zamakhshari adds that sickness often results from a person's own negligence in eating and drinking, so it is ascribed to the person, while healing, being a blessing, is ascribed to God. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi give similar explanations.

The commentators agree that medicines and physicians cure only by God's leave. Al-Razi explains illness as an imbalance of the humours, and health as a balance that only God can impose. Al-Sha'rawi holds that seeing a doctor is permitted, since the doctor is a cause while healing comes from God. Al-Razi also argues that attributing death to God in the next verse does not conflict with this courtesy, because death is a general decree that strikes everyone, whereas illness afflicts some and not others. Some Sufi-leaning authors, such as al-Sam'ani and al-Nasafi, give an inner meaning: sickness is being preoccupied with creatures and healing is witnessing the Truth. Ja'far al-Sadiq said that sickness through sins is healed by repentance. Al-Mawardi judges such readings to lie beyond the apparent meaning.

Abraham, peace be upon him, states that the One who created him, guided him, fed and gave him drink, and healed him is God alone, and that death and resurrection are in His hands: it is He who causes to die and then brings to life, and from Him he hopes for forgiveness on the Day of Judgment. The commentators read these words as an argument against his people: divinity belongs only to the one who does these things, not to idols that neither hear, benefit nor harm. On the meaning of death and life, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take them as death in this world and resurrection in the next, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan stress the final recompense, while some Sufi writers offer inner readings such as dying through sin and living through obedience, which al-Qurtubi regards as not intended by the verse. They agree that attributing death to God needs no special qualification, since no one claims to cause it, whereas Abraham attributes sickness to himself out of courtesy toward God, as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur explain. On the sin he asks to be forgiven, al-Tabari and Mujahid, followed by most, cite his three statements: 'I am sick', 'it was their chief who did this', and 'she is my sister'. Al-Zamakhshari sees them as minor lapses or prophetic humility, and Ibn Ashur as falling short of his rank. The general sense is a prayer of humility and a lesson for believers.

In this verse Abraham praises his Lord and recounts His blessings: the One who created him guides him, feeds and gives him drink, heals him when he is ill, causes him to die and then brings him back to life, and Abraham hopes that He will forgive his sin on the Day of Judgment. The commentators agree that this is an argument addressed to his people: only the one who does such things deserves worship. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Baghawi note that he attributes illness to himself out of good manners, since sickness and healing both come from God, a point also made by Qurtubi. On the word 'atma'u', most take it to mean a humble hope, while al-Hasan al-Basri takes it as certainty, a view that Razi and Baydawi reject. As for the sin, Mujahid, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy identify it with Abraham's three statements: 'I am sick', 'it was their chief who did this', and 'she is my sister'. Ibn Atiyya prefers a general reading of any lapse, while Zamakhshari, Baydawi and Alusi see minor slips or indirect remarks, since prophets are protected from major sins. Razi and Qurtubi add that the prophet's humility here teaches his community, and that forgiveness is tied to the Day of Judgment because its effect becomes visible then. Several commentators cite a hadith in Muslim in which the Prophet says that Ibn Jud'an will not benefit because he never asked for this forgiveness.

In this verse Abraham asks his Lord for a ruling, a term the commentators understand in several ways. Ibn Abbas takes it to mean knowledge and an understanding of God's limits and laws, Muqatil understanding and knowledge, Ikrima sound judgement, Mujahid the Qur'an, and al-Suddi and al-Kalbi prophethood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it as wisdom, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya as the perfection of knowledge and action. As for his request to be joined to the righteous, most read it as being placed in the rank and degree of the prophets before him, while Ibn Abbas understands the people of Paradise, and al-Zamakhshari the granting of works that link him to them or being gathered with them in Paradise. The commentators note that God answered this with the verse stating that he is among the righteous in the Hereafter.

The request for a "tongue of truth among the later generations" is generally understood as a lasting good reputation among those who come after him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that God granted it, so that all religious communities honour him. Mujahid and Qatada speak of a good praise, and Makki, reported by Ibn 'Atiyya, relates it to the coming of Muhammad, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers a fine meaning but one the wording does not readily bear. Al-Qushayri reads it as a good invocation lasting until the Hour.

The commentators observe that praise of God comes before the request, and al-Razi presents this as an important principle of supplication.

Abraham asks his Lord to give him a true and lasting good name among those who will come after him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand the phrase 'tongue of truth' as a good reputation and lasting praise. Ibn Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that this means general acceptance by the communities that follow, so that every religion honours him and speaks well of him. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say that the exegetes agree it means lasting renown and high standing, and that God answered this prayer. The word 'tongue' is a metaphor for speech, since speech is what carries a reputation, as al-Qurtubi notes quoting al-Qutaybi. Mujahid, Qatada and al-Baydawi take it as a good name that remains into the future. Another reading, given by al-Makki, al-Qushayri and Ibn Kathir, is that he asked for a righteous descendant who would uphold the truth, and that this was fulfilled in Muhammad, as al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud state. Ibn 'Atiyya considers this meaning good but says the wording of the verse does not readily support it. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi report that Imam Malik drew from this verse that it is permissible for a person to wish to be praised for righteousness, provided he seeks God's pleasure. Ibn Kathir notes that the verse 'We left for him a good name among later generations' confirms that the prayer was answered.

In this verse Abraham asks his Lord to count him among those who inherit the Garden of bliss, that is, among its people who possess it by God's grace. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the inheritance as taking the dwellings of God's enemies among the idolaters who have perished, while al-Shawkani and al-Alusi understand it as remaining in the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat the word inheritance as a metaphor for the happiness of the afterlife, which is reached only by God's grace and is compared to what is passed down as an inheritance.

The commentators agree that this request comes after his earlier prayers for wisdom, righteousness and a lasting good reputation in this world. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take the verse as permission to ask for Paradise, and they reject the view of those who say one should not ask for it. The prayer for his father in the next verse is explained by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir as made before it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of God, after which he disowned him. Al-Razi holds that the father had promised to believe, and Ibn Juzayy reports that some see the prayer as a fault or an oversight.

As for the sound heart mentioned in the following verse, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean free from polytheism or doubt, while Ibn Zayd notes that no one is free from sins. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab understands it as the healthy heart of the believer, in contrast to the heart of the disbeliever and hypocrite, al-Dahhak as the pure heart, and al-Razi as the heart free from ignorance and blameworthy traits. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy regard al-Junayd's view, that the heart is like that of one stung by a snake out of fear of God, as one of the strange interpretations.

Abraham, peace be upon him, asks his Lord to forgive his father, explaining that he was among those who had gone astray, that is, those who rejected God. The commentators agree that this plea was made before Abraham realised that his father was an enemy of God, and that when this became clear he disavowed him. Al-Razi and others mention an opinion that the father concealed his faith and showed disbelief, which would make the plea valid, but most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, hold that he died a disbeliever both outwardly and inwardly, and that the plea was a promise made to him which was later abandoned. Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith from Abu Hurayra about Abraham meeting his father on the Day of Resurrection. Regarding the request not to be humiliated on that day, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that disgrace means abasement, and some commentators say the humiliation would be seeing his father in that state. As for the sound heart, most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take it to mean free from polytheism, though Mujahid understands it as free from doubt, Ibn Sirin as believing that God is real, the Hour is coming and the dead will be raised, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab as the healthy heart of the believer. Al-Zamakhshari regards the interpretation of the heart as stung by fear of God as one of the strange interpretations, while al-Razi favours freedom from ignorance and vile character traits.

This verse gives Abraham's prayer, offered after he had praised his Lord: he asks that God not disgrace him on the Day when people are resurrected, that is, not humiliate or rebuke him before all of creation. Most commentators understand khizy as humiliation, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud also allow the sense of shame. Most take the pronoun in « yub'athun » to refer to all people, but al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi note that it may refer to the astray, in which case the request is part of his prayer for his father. The clause « the Day when neither wealth nor children will avail » is an apposition to that day: neither riches nor offspring will help on that Day. The exception is for one who comes to God with a sound heart. Scholars differ on the meaning of « sound ». Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan take it as free from polytheism, Mujahid adding freedom from doubt, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani include freedom from blameworthy innovation and sins. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reads it as the healthy heart of the believer, as opposed to the sick heart of the disbeliever and hypocrite. Al-Juneid reads it as one stung by fear of God, an interpretation al-Zamakhshari calls one of the strange readings. Al-Razi holds that the sound heart is one free of ignorance and bad character. As for the exception, some treat it as continuous and others as discontinuous, meaning « but ».

This passage states that on the Day of Resurrection, the day Abraham asked his Lord not to disgrace him, neither wealth nor children will benefit anyone. No one can ransom himself with his money or be spared punishment through his sons. The commentators broadly agree that the exception, 'except one who comes to God with a sound heart', refers to someone who meets his Lord with a heart free of associating partners with God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that most exegetes hold that no one is free of sins, so the sound heart is one preserved from shirk and doubt. Ibn Abbas defines it as the heart that testifies that there is no god but God, while al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd see it as the heart free of polytheism. Mujahid describes it as free of doubt, al-Dahhak as pure and sincere, and Ibn Abi Hatim as sincerely wishing well to God's creatures. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib says it is the healthy heart of the believer, since the heart of the disbeliever and hypocrite is diseased. Abu Uthman al-Nisaburi understands it as a heart free of innovation and at peace with the Sunna, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl as one spared the afflictions of wealth and children. Al-Junayd notes that the word salim in lexicon means 'stung', so the heart trembles out of fear of God, a reading Zamakhshari considers an odd interpretation. Al-Razi judges the most sound view to be a soul preserved from ignorance and blameworthy character. Grammarians differ on the exception: some treat it as detached, others as attached to the object of 'benefit'.

This verse records Abraham's prayer that Allah not disgrace him on the Day of Resurrection, the day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except for one who comes to Allah with a sound heart. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi largely agree that this sound heart is one free from shirk, since most commentators hold that no one is entirely free from sins. Al-Tabari reports from Mujahid that it means a heart free from doubt about Allah's oneness and the resurrection. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab understands it as the healthy heart, that of the believer, since the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. Al-Junayd reads salim in its linguistic sense of one stung by a snake, meaning a heart pierced by the fear of Allah, a reading al-Zamakhshari calls one of the odd interpretations. Al-Razi considers the most sound view to be a heart preserved from ignorance and bad character, and Ibn al-Qayyim develops the idea of a heart free from shirk, rancour, envy and attachment to the world.
