Al-Tha'alibi and Abu al-Su'ud report that some read the sound heart as free from innovation and firmly attached to the Sunnah. On grammar, the exception is read by some as connected to the subject or object, and by others as disconnected, meaning that the soundness of the heart itself benefits its owner.

This verse states that Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, meaning those who guarded themselves against disbelief and sin, so that they see it from the place of gathering and rejoice at being brought to it. Conversely, Hell will be made visible to the misguided, the polytheists, who will see it plainly and grieve at being driven toward it. The commentators explain that Paradise is brought close to the blessed, who gaze at it with delight, and that the Fire is displayed to its people, increasing their anguish. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari agree that the scene serves as a rebuke: the polytheists are asked where the deities they worshipped besides God are, and whether those deities can help them or defend themselves. Most report that these idols and their worshippers are then thrown into the Fire. Commentators differ on the meaning of the verb kubkibu: Ibn Abbas takes it to mean gathering together, Mujahid to mean hurling down, Ibn Zayd to mean casting, al-Zajjaj to mean throwing some on top of others, and Ibn Qutayba to mean being flung on their faces. On the identity of the misguided, Ibn Abbas names the polytheists, while Qatada and Muqatil name the devils. Views also vary on the armies of Iblis, understood either as his helpers among the jinn or his followers among humans. Several add that the damned will wish to return to the world to believe, a wish that cannot be granted.

The commentators explain that the verse describes Hell being brought into full view for those who went astray, meaning the disbelievers who turned away from the truth. They see it before them before entering, which increases their grief, just as the people of Paradise rejoice at drawing near to it. The misguided are, by the consensus of the opinions cited, the unbelievers and idolaters who rejected faith, defied God's prohibitions and denied His messengers, and this display belongs to the Day of Resurrection as a warning and threat.

Many opinions, transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, place this passage within a scene of the Last Day in which the idolaters are rebuked: they are asked where the deities they worshipped besides God are, and whether those deities can help them or defend themselves. The verb (fakubkibu) is explained by close meanings such as gathered, hurled, thrown on their faces or overturned. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba favour the sense that some are thrown on top of others, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the doubled root conveys the repetition of the action.

The commentators differ on who is cast down together with the deities. Ibn 'Abbas says they are the idolaters, Qatada and Muqatil say the devils, al-Suddi says the idols themselves, and al-Kalbi says the disbelievers among the jinn. As for the armies of Iblis, some take them to be his helpers among the jinn, others his followers among humans, and others his offspring. The pronoun in (fakubkibu) refers, according to Ibn 'Abbas, to the idolaters, while according to al-Suddi it refers to the idols.

This passage depicts the Day of Judgment: Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing and Hell is displayed to the misguided. The idolaters are then rebuked with a question: where are the deities you worshipped besides God, can they help you or defend themselves? The expected answer is no, they cannot. The commentators agree that this question is a reproach and a rebuke, and that the idols and their worshippers become fuel for the Fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "kubkibu" means being thrown into the Fire on top of one another, face down, again and again, while Ibn 'Abbas reads it as "gathered together". Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qutrub stress the sense of being hurled down. Opinions differ on who the "misguided" are: for Ibn 'Abbas they are the polytheists, for Qatada and Muqatil the devils, and for al-Suddi the idols themselves. The "armies of Iblis" are also read in different ways: helpers among the jinn according to some, followers among humans according to others. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that the confession of the misguided, "by God, we were in clear error", comes too late, and that their wish to return to the world will not be granted. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan observe that the past tense used here expresses certainty that the event will occur.

The commentators place this verse within the scene of the Day of Resurrection: Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, Hell is displayed to the misguided, and then the disbelievers are rebuked with a question that contains a denial: where are the things you worshipped besides God, can they help you, or can they defend themselves? The meaning is that they cannot. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the question is a rebuke and reproach that expects no answer, and its purpose is to deny any help from the idols and rivals of God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir specify that the address is to the polytheists and their idols, while several scholars hold that it covers anything worshipped besides God. On the verb "kubkibu", Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean gathered, Mujahid to be hurled down, and Ibn Zayd to be cast, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba explain it as being thrown on top of one another or on their heads. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan describe it as a doubled form of "kabba", which most philologists accept. As for the "ghawun", Ibn 'Abbas identifies them with the polytheists, Qatada and Muqatil with the devils, and al-Suddi with the deities themselves. All agree that the soldiers of Iblis are his followers among jinn and humans, and some take them to be his offspring. The commentators conclude that the scene shows the powerlessness of the idols, the regret of the idolaters, and their wish to return to the world, which will not benefit them on that day.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Judgment: Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, and Hell is displayed to the misguided. The idolaters are then rebuked with a question: where are the deities they worshipped besides God, can they help them or defend themselves? The plain meaning is that no answer comes, for the idols and the misguided are cast into the Fire. As to the word "fa-kubkibu", the commentators give closely related explanations: Ibn Abbas says they were gathered together, Mujahid that they were hurled down, Ibn Qutayba that they were overturned onto their faces or heads, and al-Zajjaj prefers that some were thrown upon others. Most agree that the root is "kubbibu", the middle letter having become a kaf, and that the doubled sound signals repeated action, each one tumbling again and again until settling at the bottom. The "misguided" are, for Ibn Abbas, the idolaters; for Qatada and Muqatil, the devils; and for al-Suddi, the deities themselves. The "hosts of Iblis" are, according to different views, his helpers among jinn and humans, or his offspring. Al-Suddi holds that the pronoun refers only to the Arab idolaters. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the plural of "intercessors" and the singular of "close friend" reflect the abundance of intercessors and the rarity of true friends.

This part of the verse says that Iblis's armies, meaning his followers and those who obeyed him in leading people astray, will be thrown into the Fire together with the false deities worshipped apart from God and with the misguided people who worshipped them, and none of them will escape. The commentators differ on who these armies are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud take them to be his devils, or his followers among jinn and humans who obeyed him. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report that they are his offspring, and al-Tabari holds that his offspring are included. Al-Mawardi gives two views: his helpers among the jinn, or his followers among humans. Ibn Ashur understands them as his allies and all kinds of error that come from his whispering. Several scholars, including Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Uthaymin, note that the word 'all' stresses totality, and Ibn Uthaymin adds that anyone who calls to misguidance is one of his soldiers. The context links the verse to the admission of the misguided that they were in clear error when they placed their idols on a par with the Lord of the worlds.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the misguided polytheists dispute in the Fire with their deities and with those who led them astray. The commentators explain that the misguided admit their clear error: they had placed their idols on a par with the Lord of the worlds in worship. Opinions differ on who the disputants are. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Muqatil identify the misguided with the devils or with the polytheists, while al-Suddi and others include the deities themselves; al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi allow that God may give the idols speech so that the dispute can take place, whereas al-Nasafi also considers a quarrel between sinners and devils. As to the statement that it was the criminals who led them astray, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur report that these may be the devils or the leaders and forefathers, with Ikrima and Abu al-Aliya naming Iblis and the first murderer, Cain, son of Adam. Nearly all agree on the sense of having no intercessors and no close friend: the intercession of angels, prophets and believers is denied to them. Al-Zamakhshari explains the singular 'friend' by its rarity and the plural 'intercessors' by their abundance. Their wish to return to the world, which will not help them, ends the passage. Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that this equating concerned love and worship, not creation.

This verse records the confession of the damned, who swear by God that they were in clear error when they made their idols equal to the Lord of the worlds in worship. The commentators agree on the general meaning: it is a sincere regret voiced once all hope has gone. As to the "criminals" who led them astray, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abi Hatim report from Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Ibn Jurayj that they are Iblis and the first murderer, the son of Adam, who first instituted killing. Al-Kalbi and Abu al-Aliya say they are their earlier ancestors whom they imitated, and Muqatil says the devils. On the "intercessors" and the "close friend", al-Tabari reports that the intercessors are the angels and the friend is a close kinsman, Ibn Jurayj adds that the intercessors are angels and the friends are people, and Qatada holds that a righteous friend benefits and a righteous intimate intercedes. Al-Zamakhshari explains the plural for intercessors and the singular for friend by the rarity of friends, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the word hamim means someone who cares deeply for us. Al-Baghawi cites the hadith of Jabir about a man asking after his friend in Paradise, and al-Razi links the passage to Abraham's supplication. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the equality concerned love, worship and submission rather than creation. Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi note the atténuative particle in and the present tense of the verb used to evoke the scene, and al-Baydawi takes the address to the idols as an expression of regret.

In this verse, the people of the Fire address the idols they used to worship besides God and admit that by equating them with the Lord of the worlds they were in manifest error. Most commentators, including al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and the Jalalayn, understand the verb as making them equal to God in worship, that is, worshipping them alongside Him. Ibn al-Qayyim clarifies that this equation was not in creation, provision, power or lordship, which the polytheists attributed to God alone, but in love, devotion, submission and reverence. Ibn Uthaymin extends worship to obeying those who declare lawful what God has forbidden, or unlawful what He has permitted. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur take the address to be directed at the idols, while Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi allow that the dialogue may be between worshippers and worshipped, or among the worshippers themselves, with the address to idols expressing intense regret. Grammatically, Abu al-Sud and al-Alusi link the temporal clause to the phrase in manifest error, though al-Alusi does not exclude a causal sense. Ibn Ashur adds that the present tense brings the scene vividly before the listener.

This verse records the words of the damned in Hell as they dispute with those they worshipped, claiming that only the criminals misled them. The commentators agree that these criminals are those who drew them into associationism and disobedience, but they differ on who exactly is meant. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur take it to mean the chiefs and great men of the people, citing the verse, 'We obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the way'. Al-Baghawi reports that Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Qatada and Ibn Juzayy identify them as the devils, while Ibn Jurayj, Ikrima and Abu al-Aliya name Iblis and Qabil, the first son of Adam who instituted murder and sins. Al-Suddi says they are the ancestors whom the people followed, a view also held by Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya. Regarding the intercessors and the close friend, al-Tabari and Ibn Jurayj understand the intercessors as angels and the close friend as a blood relative, while others, including Ibn Kathir citing Qatada, extend the intercession to prophets and believers. Al-Zamakhshari explains the grammatical choice: intercessors are many and so plural, while true friends are rare and so singular. The damned then wish to return to the world to believe, a wish that Ibn Kathir regards as insincere, since God knows they would return to what was forbidden.

This verse belongs to the words of the people of the Fire, who, having seen that their idols are of no use, lament that they have no intercessor to rescue them from punishment with God, and no close friend who cares about them. The commentators agree that the intercessors are the angels, the prophets and the believers, who will intercede on the Day of Resurrection for the faithful, while disbelievers are deprived of this intercession. Al-Tabari reports Ibn Jurayj's view that the intercessors are angels and the friend is a human, while others hold that all are human. Mujahid explains the close friend as a full brother, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi as a near relative, and Qatada says that God will remove the affection of the friend and the tenderness of the intimate on that day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain why the intercessors are plural while the friend is singular: intercessors are numerous in custom, while true friends are rare, and al-Baydawi adds that a single friend may strive more than several intercessors. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report a hadith from Jabir about a man in Paradise asking after his friend in Hell, and Ibn Kathir notes the weakness of its chain. As for their wish to return to the world and believe, Ibn Kathir explains that God knows they would revert to disobedience, and al-Zamakhshari reads the particle law as expressing a wish. Al-Alusi notes the progression of their despair, from the absence of intercessors to the absence of anyone who cares about them at all.

This verse records the words of the people of the Fire, who, cast into Hell, lament that they have neither an intercessor nor a close friend who cares for them. The commentators agree on the basic meaning: a deep regret at having no one to rescue them from punishment. They differ on who is meant. Ibn Jurayj, cited by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, holds that the intercessors are the angels and the close friend is a kinsman, while Mujahid takes the close friend to mean a full brother. Qatada, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, holds that all of them are human beings, so the damned know that a righteous friend benefits and a righteous relative intercedes. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the word intercessor implies high standing with the one being petitioned, and that the word friend implies sincere affection. On the meaning of hamim, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi connect it to caring deeply about someone, or to inner closeness, while Ibn 'Ali 'Isa, cited by al-Qurtubi, links it to the anger that a friend feels on another's behalf. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the singular 'friend' is used because true friends are rare, or because the word can stand for a group. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that the lament turns into a wish to return to the world and believe, a wish Ibn Kathir regards as insincere. Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention the hadith of Jabir about a believer who intercedes for a friend in Hell, though al-Baghawi notes that its chain of transmission is weak.

This verse records the wish of the people of the Fire to return to the world so that they might believe, after realising they have no intercessor and no true friend. The commentators explain that "karra" means a return to this life, and that "law" here expresses a wish like "laytа", with "fa-nakun" as its answer; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also note it may be a conditional whose answer is omitted, meaning we would then have done such and such good deeds. Nearly all agree the verse shows late regret once hope has gone. On who the intercessors are, al-Tabari reports that Ibn Juraij took them to be angels and the close friend to be a human, while Mujahid understood a full brother and Qatada held that righteous relatives and friends can indeed intercede. al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi cite a hadith of Jabir about a man asking after his friend in Hell, though not all accept its soundness. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that the disbelievers thought their idols would intercede or that their human allies among the devils would help them. Al-Zamakhshari explains the plural "intercessors" and singular "friend" by the frequency of intercessors and the rarity of friends. Al-Razi also records al-Jubba'i's view that the wish expresses resolve rather than a real commitment to faith, whereas Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin argue that a return would not in fact produce belief, as the verse in al-An'am indicates. Overall the passage conveys the regret of the disbelievers and the absence of any intercession, while the commentators differ on who the intercessors are and on the precise force of the wish.

This verse states that the story of Abraham with his people, and the fate awaiting idol worshippers on the Day of Resurrection, is a sign for whoever reflects, and that most people, whether Abraham's people according to some or the Quraysh according to others, did not believe. God is mighty and able to punish, yet merciful in granting respite for repentance. The commentators describe the otherworldly scene evoked in the preceding verses: Paradise brought near to the God-fearing and Hellfire displayed to the misguided, then the deities and their worshippers are hurled into the fire together with all of Iblis's hosts. They dispute, acknowledge their error in setting their gods on a par with the Lord of the worlds, and shift the blame onto the criminals who led them astray. Most say these are the devils, al-Suddi says the ancestors they followed, and Ibn Jurayj, Abu al-'Aliya and 'Ikrima say Iblis and Cain, the first to institute killing.

The commentators agree that disbelievers have no intercessor or friend who benefits them, while believers intercede for one another. They differ on the intercessors: some hold they are the angels, while Ibn Jurayj adds humans for the friend. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the friend means a close relative, and az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the plural for intercessors and the singular for friend reflect the frequency of the former and the rarity of the latter. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi cite Jabir's report of the man asking after his friend in Paradise, which al-Baghawi notes has a weak chain. Their wish to return to the world is seen as sincere by some, but al-Razi and al-Baydawi point out that God announces they would relapse into what they were forbidden.

Al-Razi sees in this verse a consolation for the Prophet facing the rejection of his people.

This verse closes the account of Abraham's argument with his people and the scene of the Day of Judgment, stating that your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Al-Tabari explains that the Mighty is the one who severely punishes whoever worships others besides Him and dies without repenting, while the Merciful does not punish, for the sins committed before repentance, those who turn back to Him. Al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani understand the Mighty as the one who cannot be overcome, and al-Sha'rawi adds that His might is joined with mercy, since He opens the door of repentance to those who return. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the Mighty is able to hasten punishment, while the Merciful grants respite so that the people, or some of their descendants, may believe. Al-Nasafi gives a concrete sense: the Mighty takes revenge on those who denied Abraham by casting them into the fire of Hell, and the Merciful brings every sound heart to the garden of bliss. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a third repetition of a refrain already used in the surah, meant to record the stubbornness of the polytheists and to show that the proof of God's oneness is clear. The commentators agree that the verse consoles the Prophet over his people's rejection, and that divine mercy does not cancel divine might or punishment.

The commentators explain that Noah's people denied their prophet Noah, and that the plural "the messengers" is used because rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, since their call is the same and the basics of their laws do not differ. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi also note that the plural may refer to Noah alone, following a familiar Arabic usage. Noah told his people that he was their brother by lineage and not by religion, that he was a trustworthy messenger known for his honesty among them, and he called them to fear God and obey him. He said he asked them for no wage, since his reward lies with the Lord of the worlds. They replied: "Shall we believe you, when the lowliest follow you?" He answered that the knowledge of their deeds was not his concern, that their reckoning belongs to his Lord, that he would not drive away the believers, and that he was only a clear warner. On the meaning of "the lowliest," Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Jawzi understood them to be craftsmen of humble trades such as weavers, cuppers or cobblers, while al-Qurtubi held that the contempt concerned their conduct and standing in the eyes of the disbelievers, and Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan considered them poor or lowly people. Most commentators report the threat of stoning, Noah's prayer for deliverance, the rescue in the laden ship and the drowning of the rest. Ibn Kathir states that Noah was the first messenger sent to earth, while Ibn Uthaymin considers that his mission reached all people by circumstance rather than by intention.

This verse recounts Noah's words to his people when he called them to fear God and abandon the worship of other beings. He told them he was their brother by lineage rather than by faith, and that he was a trustworthy messenger sent from God. The commentators agree that the passage contains a clear call to monotheism and obedience, and that Noah asked his people for no payment, his reward resting with God alone. They all hold that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, since their message is the same, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain, and some read the plural "messengers" as referring to the category as a whole.

The meaning of kinship receives several readings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it as a bond of lineage. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that it can also be a bond of shared belonging, as when the Arabs said "O brother of Banu Tamim". As for Noah's trustworthiness, some understand it as a reputation for integrity among his people, like Muhammad's among Quraysh, while others read it as faithfulness in conveying the revelation. Regarding the "lowly ones" who followed him, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report differing views: they were people of humble trades such as weavers, cuppers or cobblers, whereas al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya consider that the insult targeted their modest social standing and means more than their crafts.

Finally, the threat of being "stoned" is understood by Qatada and Ibn Abbas as death by stones or death in general, and by al-Suddi as mere abuse.

This passage tells us that the people of Noah denied him, though he was a single messenger, and so in effect they denied all the messengers, since their message is one in its core, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain. The phrase "I am a trustworthy messenger to you" is read by the commentators as meaning a messenger of God faithful in conveying the revelation without addition or omission, and one already known for his honesty among his people, as al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi report. Most understand the brotherhood mentioned as one of lineage rather than of faith, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that it can also mean a shared origin, as in the phrase "O brother of Tamim".

Noah urges his people to fear God and obey him, and says he asks them for no wage, his reward resting with the Lord of the worlds, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di point out. When the chiefs answer by asking why they should believe when the "lowliest" are following him, the commentators differ on who these were: al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi say they were people of low station, and several report they were weavers, cuppers or cobblers, a view al-Qurtubi considers unfounded. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests the charge was one of moral contempt, while al-Razi calls the objection very weak, since the mission is addressed to all. Noah replies that he does not know their deeds and that their reckoning is up to his Lord. Finally, their threat to stone him is read by some as execution by stones and by others as mere abuse.

This passage records Noah's command to his people to fear God and obey him. The commentators explain that the meaning is to guard against God's punishment by abandoning idolatry and polytheism, and to obey Noah in his call to monotheism and his sincere counsel. The command is repeated to fix it in their hearts: the first is justified by Noah's trustworthiness among them, the second by his refusal to ask any reward, since his wage rests with the Lord of the worlds. All agree that the brotherhood mentioned is one of lineage rather than faith, and that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, since their message is the same. They differ, however, on the meaning of the word "al-arḏalūn" with which the people answered Noah. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean craftsmen in lowly trades such as weavers, cuppers or cobblers, while others read it simply as people of low station and poverty. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the insult targeted their conduct rather than their trades, whereas al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari say the notables despised them for their poverty and humble birth. Noah replied that he does not know their works, that their reckoning belongs to his Lord, and that he is only a plain warner. The threat of stoning is understood by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi as death by stones, while others take it as mere reviling. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the command to fear God comes first because it is the cause of obedience.

This passage recounts Noah's mission to his people, who rejected him although he was their brother by descent rather than by faith. He called them to fear God and obey him, affirmed his trustworthiness as a messenger, and stated that he asked them for no reward, since his recompense rests with the Lord of the worlds alone. The commentators agree that rejecting Noah amounts to rejecting all the messengers, since their call is one, and that repeating the command to fear God and obey him reinforces the message, each command being tied to a reason: his trustworthiness first, and the denial of any personal gain second. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that disclaiming any wage removes the suspicion that the call serves a worldly interest. The people objected that his followers were the lowliest. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that these were people of humble status or low crafts such as weavers, cuppers and cobblers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the insult targeted the believers' conduct rather than their trades, and al-Qurtubi finds the idea that a craft harms faith untenable. Noah replied that he was not charged with knowing their deeds, that their reckoning belongs to his Lord, and that he would not drive away the believers, being only a clear warner. Ibn 'Ashur notes that this story consoles the Prophet, since the Quraysh treated his companions in the same way. Al-Sha'rawi observes that seeking reward only from God keeps the call above worldly motives.

In this verse Noah urges his people to fear God and obey him, after assuring them that he is a trustworthy messenger who asks them for no wage, since his reward rests with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that the repetition serves to reinforce the message in their hearts. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the fear of God as guarding oneself against his punishment, while al-Razi and Ibn Ashur read the two commands as distinct appeals, one grounded in Noah's trustworthiness and the other in his disinterestedness. Al-Zamakhshari notes that each command is tied to a reason, and that fear of God comes first because it is the cause of obedience. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi observe that the kinship between Noah and his people is one of descent, not of faith. The scornful reply of the notables, who object that the lowly follow him, is reported by al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, who give several readings of who these people were: beggars, the lowborn, or craftsmen such as weavers and cuppers. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya treat the craft explanation as an example rather than a restriction. Noah replies that he does not know their inner deeds and that their reckoning rests with God alone. Al-Qasimi attributes their refusal to the contempt of the wealthy for the poor, and Ibn Kathir sees in the verse a call to the oneness of God.

This passage records the reply of Noah's people: how can we believe you when those who follow you are the lowly, the poor and the common? The commentators give several meanings to the word al-arḏalūn. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima took it to mean weavers and cobblers, others goldsmiths or cuppers, Qatada and Muqatil the lowest of people, and 'Ata' the destitute with neither wealth nor standing. Al-Mawardi also lists beggars who are never content and the arrogant. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya compare this attitude with that of the Quraysh towards the Prophet's companions, citing the hadith of Heraclius that the followers of prophets are generally the weak. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi regard contempt for trades as ignorant, since crafts do not harm faith. Ibn 'Atiyya thinks the scorn targets the conduct of believers rather than their trades. Noah replies that he is not charged with knowing their deeds; he sees only their outward state, and their reckoning rests with God, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri add that the notables wanted him to drive the believers away. All agree that Noah answers that he is a clear warner and will not drive the believers off. The notables then threaten him with stoning, which Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn 'Abbas take as being killed by stones, while others read it as being reviled.

This verse records Noah's reply to his people, who objected that they would not believe in him when only the lowliest had followed him. He says he has no knowledge of what those followers did, and that his duty is only to judge by outward appearances and to call to faith, while their reckoning lies with their Lord alone. The commentators agree that the "lowliest" were the poor and the humble in the eyes of the people, and that Noah declines to probe their inner secrets. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the leaders wanted him to drive the believers away before they would follow him, and he refuses, presenting himself as a clear warner. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the leaders doubted the sincerity of these believers, whom they thought had accepted out of desire and impulse, and Noah answers that true wealth is the wealth of religion and true lineage is that of piety. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan understand the insult as aimed at their conduct rather than their trades. As for the trades named, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi mention weavers, cobblers, smiths and barbers, but al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi insist that a craft does not harm one's faith. Ibn Ashur and al-Zamakhshari read the phrase "if you knew" as a rebuke of their ignorance. Finally, regarding the threat of stoning, some commentators take it literally and others as insult, and al-Qurtubi notes both readings.

This verse records Noah's reply to his people, who had asked whether they should believe in him when the most despised people were the ones following him. He answers that he is not responsible for knowing the inner deeds and intentions of his followers; he only judges their outward state, and their account rests with their Lord. Had they perceived this, they would not have looked down on them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as Noah leaving the hearts to God, while al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the prophet's duty is to judge by appearances. On who the 'most despised' were, the commentators differ. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan record several views: weavers, cuppers, cobblers, or people of lowly trades, a view ascribed to Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrimah. Others, such as Qatada and Ibn 'Ashur, understand them as the poor, the weak and the lowly in society, the usual target of the elite's contempt. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi suggest that Noah pretended not to grasp their meaning and redefined baseness as bad conduct and corrupt beliefs, adding that wealth and trade do not diminish a believer in God's eyes, and that piety, not lineage, is the true nobility. Al-Qurtubi notes the recitation variants, where some read the verb 'you perceive' and others 'they perceive', and the omitted answer of the conditional 'law', which is understood as 'you would have ceased to blame them'.

This passage from the story of Noah, peace be upon him, shows that he refused to drive away the believers who followed him. He says it is not his place to yield to his people's demand, since he is a clear warner charged with delivering the message, not with judging people's hidden hearts. The commentators explain the phrase 'the most despicable' used by his opponents in different ways. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that it refers to weavers, cobblers or goldsmiths, that is, to trades regarded as lowly. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the contempt was directed mainly at the believers' conduct and poverty rather than their crafts, and that faith removes no honour from its followers. Al-Zamakhshari argues that Noah used the word 'lowly' by his own standard, meaning bad conduct and corrupt beliefs, not by his people's standard. Al-Razi, for his part, considers the objection very weak, since the mission addresses everyone regardless of wealth or trade. As for the words 'I do not know what they did', al-Tabari explains that Noah was not required to know their hidden intentions, only their outward appearance. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean that the matter rests with God. The meaning of 'their reckoning' is also debated: for al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir it concerns their deeds, while others see it as their inner sincerity. Regarding the threat of being stoned, Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil read it as death by stones, Qatada as being struck with stones, and Dahhak as being insulted.

This part of the verse has Noah declare that his role is limited to clear warning: he is a plain warner who sets out clearly what he was sent with, without judging people's inner states or driving away those who followed him. The commentators read the verse within the exchange with his people, who asked him to expel his poorer followers, so his words are a reply to that demand. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that it is his task only to warn them with clear proof that distinguishes truth from falsehood, after which each person is accountable for his own conduct. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that a plain warning cannot be used to please some by pushing others away. Al-Razi and al-Alusi take the clause as the reason for refusing to expel the believers: his mission is to warn all people, so whoever accepts is near and whoever rejects is far. Al-Zamakhshari adds that true wealth is the wealth of faith and true nobility is that of piety. The commentators agree that 'mubin' means clear, not hiding any part of the message, and Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that it may also be read in the active sense of one who makes his message manifest. Most of them draw no legal ruling from this passage and confine themselves to the meaning and the context of the dialogue.

This verse reports that Noah's people, unable to answer his arguments after a long mission of calling them day and night, turned to threats: if he did not stop calling them and reviling their gods, they said, he would be among those stoned. The commentators broadly agree that "al-marjumin" means those who will be pelted with stones and killed, as Qatada, Muqatil, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. Al-Sudi and al-Dahhak take it to mean being reviled, the stoning being figurative of abuse, a view echoed by al-Alusi and al-Tha'alibi, who compare it to the figurative use of stabbing for slander. Ibn Atiyya considers that the word may carry either sense, while Ibn Uthaymin favours literal stones, arguing that insult is rarely used and does not suit people who regard themselves as powerful. The commentators place this threat near the end of the dispute, when Noah had despaired of their faith. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Razi stress that Noah did not seek personal revenge but defended his religion. Ibn Ashur sees such threats as the usual recourse of those defeated by argument. The commentators then report that Noah turned to God in supplication, after which he and the believers were saved in the ark while the rest were drowned.

This verse records the supplication of Noah, peace be upon him, after his people threatened to stone him. He complains to his Lord that they denied him, and asks Him to judge between him and them with a judgment that destroys the liars and saves Noah and the believers with him. The commentators explain fath as judgment and decision: Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it as a ruling between Noah and his people, while al-Tabari understands it as a judgment that destroys the wrongdoer and punishes the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani relate that this prayer came after a long period of preaching and despair of their faith, God having told him that only those who had already believed would believe. All agree that the laden ship (al-fulk al-mashhun) is the filled vessel, and that the drowning followed the rescue of the believers. On the meaning of al-marjumin, Qatada says stoning, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil say killing, and al-Suddi says insult; al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur favour stoning or insult. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain that Noah was not informing God of something He already knew, but meant that they had rejected his revelation and mission, and that his plea concerned the religion rather than the harm done to him. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani understand the judgment here as the destruction of the people.

This verse records Noah's prayer after his people threatened to stone him. He complains to his Lord that they have denied him and asks Him to judge between him and them with a decisive judgment, meaning that the deniers should be destroyed and that he and the believers with him should be saved. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain that "fataḥ" means to judge or decide, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the fattah to be the judge, and al-Sam'ani cites an Arabic verse using the word in this sense. All agree that this judgment includes the destruction of the disbelievers and the rescue of the believers; al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the phrase "and save me" shows that punishment of the people is intended. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the believers who were with Noah were few, and al-Qurtubi names them as his sons, wives, daughters-in-law and grandsons, though the scholars differ on whether others were among them. On the word "denied", al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that Noah had been told that none of his people would believe except those who already had, and that he then prayed against them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that this is not information given to God, who knows all, but an explanation of the reason for the prayer, since Noah sought justice for his religion rather than revenge for the harm done to him. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur link the verse to the accounts of the flood to describe its outcome.

The commentators explain that God saved Noah and those who were with him, after answering his prayer to judge between him and his people, and that "the laden ark" means the ship filled to capacity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the word "open" (fath) as a judgment, that is, the sending of punishment, and al-Razi argues that the rescue would make no sense without the destruction of the disbelievers. As for the word "laden", most agree that it means full or heavily loaded: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada speak of a ship filled or loaded, and al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya specify that it was filled with people, birds and animals. Ibn Kathir notes that a pair of every kind was taken aboard, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the singular "the ship" here stands for a large number of passengers. All agree that the drowning of the others came after the salvation. Ibn Ashur explains that "then" (thumma) marks a difference in rank here, since the destruction of an entire people is a greater sign of divine power than the rescue of a small group.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of Noah: after God saved Noah and those who believed with him in the laden ship, He drowned the rest of his people, who had rejected his message and his warning. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain that the word mashhun means loaded, full or heavily burdened, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that the ship carried people, animals and various provisions, while al-Qurtubi considers that its passengers were Noah, his offspring and his followers. The exegetes agree that the word al-baqin refers to those among Noah's people who remained in disbelief, and that the drowning took place after the believers were saved. Ibn Ashur sees in the particle thumma a gradation of rank, since the destruction of an entire nation shows God's power more clearly than the rescue of a group. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi report that Noah prayed against his people only after being told that none of them would believe further, and al-Razi stresses that his supplication was for the sake of religion and not for personal revenge. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di emphasise the lesson to be drawn from this outcome for those who deny the message.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the story of Noah: in the rescue of Noah and those with him in the loaded ark, and the drowning of the rest of his people, there is a great sign, and most of that people were not believers. Al-Tabari applies the lesson first to the Prophet Muhammad and his people: God's custom is to save His messengers and their followers and to destroy those who deny them, and the fact that most would not believe had already been decreed by God. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others take "most of them" to refer to Noah's people, while Ibn 'Uthaymin says the more correct reading is that it refers to those to whom the Prophet was sent, though he notes that the author he cites took it to mean Noah's people. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a warning to the Quraysh, who knew the story of the flood. On the "laden ship", Ibn 'Abbas said it means full or heavily loaded, 'Ata' said weighed down, and Mujahid said filled. The passage then moves to the story of 'Ad, where Hud speaks the same words of piety and trustworthiness as Noah. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that Noah's request for judgment between himself and his people was not a personal grievance but a plea for the sake of his religion. Al-Razi adds that Noah only prayed for their destruction after being told that none of them would believe beyond those who already had.

This verse states that God is the Mighty, who punishes those who disbelieve in Him and disobey His command, and the Merciful, especially toward the repentant and the believers. It closes the story of Noah and his people. Commentators explain that the rescue of Noah and the believers in the laden ship, and the drowning of the rest, is a sign for the Prophet and his people, and that God's pattern of saving the messengers and their followers while destroying those who deny them is constant. The small number of believers was already known to God.

The commentators agree on the apparent meaning: the drowning came after the believers were saved, and both God's power and His mercy are plainly stated. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Uthaymeen stress that might brings vengeance on the deniers while mercy protects the believers. Al-Tabari adds that the mercy applies to the penitent who is not punished after repenting. Ibn Uthaymeen also holds that mercy is a real attribute of God, and he distinguishes three senses of might: greatness, dominance and inaccessibility to harm.

The disagreement concerns the reference of "most of them". Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi take it to mean the contemporaries of the Prophet, Ibn Uthaymeen says the more correct view is that it refers to those to whom the messenger was sent, while Abu al-Su'ud finds it far-fetched to refer it to most of Noah's people. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a lesson for the Quraysh, who knew the story of the Flood.

This verse states that the people of 'Ad, the tribe of Hud, denied their messenger, and that this denial amounts to denying all the messengers, since their call shared the same foundations, as al-Shawkani and al-Sa'di explain. The commentators note that 'Ad was originally the name of their forefather, later applied to the tribe, which is why the verb is feminine, as al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur point out. The word "brother" refers to Hud by lineage rather than by religion, according to al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi. Hud urges his people to fear God and obey him, declares himself a trustworthy messenger, and affirms that he asks them for no wage, his reward resting with the Lord of the worlds; this point is agreed upon. On the specific things he rebukes them for, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi, followed by al-Tabari, take the word "rey'" to mean a road or a high place, while Mujahid understands a pass between two mountains and others pigeon towers. For "masani'", Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas say fortified palaces, Qatada water reservoirs, and al-Sudi pigeon towers. Al-Zamakhshari finds the palace reading most apparent, while Ibn Kathir reads the building as pointless vanity. For "la'allakum takhludun", Ibn 'Abbas reads it as "as if you were eternal", al-Farra' as "so that you may remain", and Ibn Zayd as a question of reproach. The word "batsh" means for Mujahid whipping and killing with the sword, and for al-Kalbi and al-Hasan killing in anger. Al-Razi links these traits to love of height, permanence and domination, which he regards as the root of every fault, though he presents this as his own reading.

This passage from Surat al-Shu'ara' recounts the call of the prophet Hud to his people 'Ad. His brother by lineage asks them whether they will not fear God. He presents himself as a trustworthy messenger from his Lord, urges them to fear God and obey him, and says he asks them for no wage, his reward resting with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that the call concerns the oneness of God and the abandonment of idolatry, and that describing Hud as trustworthy shows he was known for integrity before his mission, as Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Juzayy note. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi explain that 'brother' means kinship by lineage, not by religion.

The word rayʿ in the next phrase is usually taken to mean a high place, as al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold, while Qatada, al-Dahhak and Muqatil say it means a road, and Mujahid a pass between two mountains; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record other meanings. Opinions also differ on the 'sign' the people build: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as a landmark, Mujahid as dovecotes, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi as tall buildings. The mașani' are read by some as fortified palaces and by others as water reservoirs. The phrase 'so that you may live forever' is read by some as 'as if you were to live forever' and by others as mockery.

The commentators agree in condemning vain building, arrogance and unjust violence, and al-Razi and Abu Hayyan see in these an attachment to height and survival. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note the reading of the word khuluq in the phrase about the ancients. Some take it as the custom of the ancients, others as their fabrications, and both senses are reported by the commentators cited.

This passage recounts the call of Hud to his people, 'Ad. He tells them he is their brother by lineage, not in religion, that he is a messenger from his Lord and a trustworthy one in what he conveys, and he urges them to fear God and obey him. He states that he asks them for no wage, since his reward rests only with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri, agree that the verse affirms the trustworthiness and disinterestedness of the prophets. Al-Kalbi held that his trustworthiness was known before his mission, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari stress that 'brother' means kinship by descent. On the following phrase about towering structures, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and others take the rī' to be a high road or elevated place, Mujahid a pass between two mountains or dovecotes, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir describe monuments built for display and idle play. Al-Razi sees these acts as signs of love for height and permanence. As for the 'fortresses', some explain them as water reservoirs and others as fortified palaces. The 'tyrants' are, for the commentators, those who strike with the sword or whip without right, a blameworthy conduct. The exegetes conclude that true calling rests on piety, obedience and refusing any payment.

In this verse, Hud, who was a brother of the 'Ad by lineage, calls his people to fear God and obey him. He presents himself as a trustworthy messenger sent to them and states that he asks no wage for his message, since his reward rests with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that fearing God means dreading his punishment by abstaining from polytheism and sins, and that obedience means accepting what he conveys from his Lord. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that he was their brother by descent and not in religion, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur add that he was known for trustworthiness before his mission, as al-Kalbi reports. Ibn 'Ashur observes that a prophet is only sent once he is known for integrity. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir connect this call to the rebuke about their tall constructions. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'ri'': Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi take it to be a road, Ibn 'Abbas also a high place, and Mujahid a pass between two mountains or dovecotes, while some hold that they built on high ground to mock passers-by. The 'masani'' are described as fortified palaces by some and water reservoirs by others, and 'la'allakum takhludun' is read either as 'as if you would live forever', as 'so that you might live forever', or as a rhetorical question of reproach. Readings of 'khuluq al-awwalin' vary between custom, creation and fabrication, depending on the reading tradition.

This verse records the words of the prophet Hud to his people, the 'Ad: he tells them that he asks no payment for calling them to fear God and obey him, since his reward rests only with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators broadly agree that this shows the messenger's sincerity and disinterest. Al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain that the prophetic mission is based solely on calling people to know the truth and obey, and that the prophets are free from worldly aims. Al-Shawkani notes that Noah had said the same before him. Al-Sha'rawi observes that Abraham and Moses did not use this phrase, because of their family ties with their listeners. Ibn 'Uthaymin focuses on the word 'ala' (upon): God owes nothing, but may bind himself to reward out of generosity, and Ibn al-Qayyim, whom he cites, makes the reward depend on sincerity and good action. In the following verses Hud rebukes his people for building high structures without need, out of vanity and play, and for their violence. Commentators differ on the meaning of 'rī'' (a high place, a road, a mountain pass) and of 'āya' (a landmark or a building). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi share these readings, while stressing the futility of such constructions.

The Qur'an reports Hud's words to his people 'Ad: do you build a landmark on every high place, playing at it? On the meaning of 'rī' (ri'), Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Qatada take it as a road, while Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' also give the sense of a raised place; Mujahid speaks of a pass between two mountains or a small defile. The word 'āya' is read by some as a sign or tall structure, by others as dovecotes. Most commentators agree that 'ʿabath' means play and useless activity. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi report that these buildings showed off strength and pride, while others say they were used to mock passers-by. The 'maṣāni' are, according to Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, fortified palaces; according to Qatada, water reservoirs; according to al-Suddi, dovecotes. For 'la'allakum takhludun', Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain it as 'as if you would remain forever', al-Farra' as 'so that you may live forever', and Ibn Zayd reads it as a rebuking question. As for 'baṭashtum', Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj understand killing by sword and beating with whips, while al-Kalbi and al-Hasan understand killing in anger without reflection. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi hold that, lacking decisive evidence, the general sense of the maṣāni' should be kept, and al-Zamakhshari finds the palace interpretation more evident than the signpost one.

This passage records Hud's words to his people 'Ad. He rebukes them for building a landmark on every height in a pointless way, for constructing edifices as if they would live forever, and for striking people with the violence of tyrants. The commentators agree on the general meaning: it is a condemnation of vanity, of attachment to pleasure, and of heedlessness toward the Hereafter. The details, however, differ. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir take 'rî'' to mean a high place, Mujahid a pass between two mountains, and Qatada and others a road. Ibn 'Abbas understands 'āya' as a landmark, while Mujahid understands dovecotes or buildings. According to Mujahid and Ibn Kathir the 'masani'' are solid palaces or fortresses, according to Qatada water reservoirs, and according to al-Kalbi dwellings. On 'la'allakum takhludun', most read it as 'as if you were to remain' or 'hoping to remain'. Ibn Zayd reads it as a rhetorical question of reproach, and al-Farra' as meaning 'so that'. As for violence, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid speak of whipping and killing by the sword unjustly, whereas al-Hasan and al-Kalbi describe killing in anger without reflection. Al-Razi links these three traits to a love of height, of permanence, and of sole dominion.

Hud, peace be upon him, rebukes his people, the 'Ad, for two things: building landmarks on every high place in vain play, and erecting fortified buildings as if they would live forever. Then comes the phrase: 'And when you strike, you strike like tyrants', meaning that when they seized someone they did so with violence and force. The commentators broadly agree on the meaning of striking (al-batsh) as forceful seizure. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy understand it as harming others by force. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid specify killing by the sword or beating with a whip, al-Kalbi and al-Hasan add that it means killing in anger without reflection, and Yahya ibn Salam speaks of unjust killing by the sword. Al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi describe punishment without mercy or any aim of correction. Al-Mawardi also mentions, as a further possibility, punishment without pardon or leniency. Ibn 'Atiyya defines the jabbar as the arrogant domineering person. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di note that these people had been given great strength which they did not use in obedience. Thus, across the commentaries, the verse warns against tyranny and brutality and calls for the fear of God and obedience to the Messenger.

Hud urges his people, the 'Ad, to fear God and obey him in what he commands. He reminds them that God has provided them with blessings they know well: livestock, sons, gardens and springs, and warns them of the punishment of a terrible day if they persist in disbelief. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Jalalayn agree that the fear of God means avoiding polytheism and sins, and that obedience means obeying the messenger in what he conveys from his Lord. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that this command follows the condemnation of vain building and of tyranny toward people. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that fear of God is placed before obedience because it is its cause. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di see in the reminder of blessings a reason for piety, since the one who bestows a favour deserves gratitude and obedience. The commentators do not differ on the essential meaning of the verse; their differences concern mainly the nature of the blessings listed, with gardens and springs understood by some as orchards and rivers, and by Ibn 'Ashur as the source of the people's comfort and abundant provision. Several add that the preaching of hope and warning did not move this people, who replied that the admonition meant nothing to them, and that God destroyed them with a violent wind.

Hud, peace be upon him, urges his people of ʿAd to fear God and obey him, then asks them to fear the One who has supplied them with blessings they know well. After first mentioning these blessings in general terms, he names them in detail: livestock, sons, gardens and flowing springs. The commentators present these favours as proof against them, since the one who grants them deserves to be feared and obeyed, and he warns them of the punishment of a great day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Saʿdi agree on this general sense, while al-Baydawi and al-Alusi see the repetition as a way of reminding and emphasising. Ibn ʿAshur explains that livestock come first because they sustain life, then sons, who help in tending them and keep the name alive, then gardens and springs, which bring comfort. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that naming the palm trees after the gardens may be a case of singling out a part within the general. The verse carries no notable legal ruling; its main lesson is that blessings call for gratitude. Commentators also note Hud's gentleness, as he speaks to them as a brother of their lineage, while his people remain indifferent to his warnings.

Hud reminds his people, 'Ad, of the blessings God has given them. He says that the One who supplied them with what they know, namely livestock, sons, gardens and springs, deserves their fear and obedience, and he warns them of the punishment of a great day if they persist in disbelief. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: a reminder of a favour that calls for gratitude and piety. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that 'livestock' means camels, cattle and sheep, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that sons are mentioned alongside livestock because they help to tend them. Ibn 'Ashur explains that livestock come first because they were the most precious wealth of that land. The people's reply was contemptuous: for them, whether he admonishes or not makes no difference, and what he says is only the custom of the ancients. The readers differ over 'khuluq' and 'khalq': al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the reading with a fatha means lies and invention, while the reading with a damma means the custom or religion of the ancients. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that this speech amounts to denying the resurrection. The commentators finally recall that God destroyed them with a furious wind, a sign for those who reflect.

The plain meaning of 'gardens and springs' is that Hud, peace be upon him, lists for his people of 'Ad the blessings God had given them, mentioning gardens and watercourses among them. The commentators explain the gardens as orchards and the springs as rivers or flowing water, as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi, al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti do, while Ibn Kathir describes these people as having great strength and prosperity. All of them connect these gifts to the livestock and sons mentioned just before, and place the verse within a reminder of blessings and a warning of a terrible day.

Al-Zamakhshari observes that listing the blessings after a general mention awakens the heedless and makes them recognise their Benefactor. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud see the detail as strengthening the exhortation. Ibn 'Ashur explains the order: livestock are the basis of livelihood, sons are support and the continuation of a name, while gardens and springs bring comfort and an abundance of provision. Al-Alusi finds the pairing of gardens with springs clearly fitting, since water completes the blessing of an orchard.

The commentators largely agree on the meaning of these two words; they differ only in how they phrase the springs, speaking of streams, springs or rivers. The general sense remains constant: God gave the 'Ad wealth, greenery and water, which should lead them to fear and thank Him.

This verse records Hud's exhortation to his people, 'Ad. He commands them to fear God and obey him, reminds them of the blessings they received (livestock, sons, gardens and springs), and warns them of the punishment of a tremendous day. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, understand this punishment as the destruction that struck them in this world, though Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan also mention, as a possibility, punishment in the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the warning covers both this life and the next, because ingratitude for blessings brings punishment. Al-Nasafi and the authors of the Jalalayn link the fear to the condition of disobedience. Al-Razi notes that the blessings are first named in summary and then in detail, and that livestock is paired with sons because sons help in tending it. On the meaning of 'a tremendous day', the commentators agree that it is a day of great terror. As for the people's reply, 'it is all the same to us whether you admonish us or not', al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read it as indifference to his warning. Ibn 'Ashur points out that the expression of fear shows Hud's compassion for his people, who were his own kin. There is no notable disagreement about the general sense of the verse, which is a warning to a people who rejected their prophet.

This verse reports the reply of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud after he had warned them and urged them to fear God and obey him. They say that his admonition and its absence are the same to them, meaning they will not turn back from what they do and pay no heed to his words. The commentators read this as an expression of contempt and obstinacy. Hud had reminded them of God's favours, cattle, sons, gardens and springs, and warned them of a terrible day. Most exegetes define waʿz as speech that softens the heart through promise and threat. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the balanced form of the phrase is stronger than a simple 'whether you admonish or not', as it shows how little they value his words.

Their words, 'this is only the custom of the ancients', are read differently. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ikrima and al-Tabari take them to mean the religion or custom of the ancestors, that they live and die as their forefathers did with no resurrection. Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and others take the word as meaning invention or lies. Some scholars accept both senses, since the two recitations allow either. Ibn Kathir favours the sense of custom and belief, and their denial of punishment is read as a denial of resurrection.

The story ends, as the commentators explain, with their rejection of Hud and their destruction by a violent wind, a sign for those who reflect, though most of them did not believe.

The commentators explain that when the people of Hud were admonished by their prophet, reminded of God's favours and warned of a tremendous day, they replied that his preaching and his silence were the same to them, and then claimed that what they followed was only the custom of the ancients and that they would not be punished for it. The exegetes agree that the verse depicts the arrogant attitude of this people toward admonition.

The meaning of khuluq is debated. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand it as the religion or custom of the ancients, while al-Farra' takes it as their way of life. Mujahid, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Zamakhshari, reading khalq with an open khaa, read it as lies and fabrication. Al-Mawardi reports a related reading in which Qatada took it to mean that the ancients died without being raised. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the reading with two dammas, arguing that the people of 'Ad acknowledged a Creator and worshipped idols, which explains their words that they would not be punished.

Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the phrase sawa'un 'alayna and the wording am lam takun min al-wa'izin form an intensifier of their scorn, al-Zamakhshari stressing that this is stronger than am lam ta'iz. Ibn 'Ashur explains that khuluq denotes a disposition firmly rooted in the soul and can thus designate an inherited habit.

As for the outcome, the commentators agree that their rejection led to their destruction by a violent wind. Ibn Kathir specifies that it blew for seven nights and eight days. Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that the verse invites the believer to reflect on the fate of peoples who denied their prophets.

The commentators explain that the people of 'Ad, when their prophet Hud admonished them and warned them of a terrible day, replied that whether he admonished them or not made no difference to them, and that what they did was merely the custom of the ancients, and that they would not be punished. The exegetes agree that their words "and we shall not be punished" are a denial of the threat Hud had made, revealing their confidence in their own strength. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that this statement follows their reply directly, reaffirming their rejection of the announced punishment. Al-Tabari, with Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, understands "khuluq al-awwalin" as the religion and practices of the forefathers, the reading he prefers, while Ibn Kathir reports that others, including Mujahid, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Alqama, took it to mean fabrication and lies. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi set out both readings and their meanings. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba note that the Arabs used the word khalq for invented tales, so the term can carry both senses. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the demonstrative may refer to their way of life or to Hud's message, and that the phrase may explain their scorn for the admonition. The commentators do not choose between these readings, each presenting what the text can bear. Ibn Kathir adds that the destruction came through a violent, bitterly cold wind, as the Quran describes elsewhere.

Verse 139 of Surat ash-Shu'ara concludes the story of 'Ad, the people who denied their brother Hud. God says that He destroyed them because of their denial, that this is a sign, and that most of them were not believers. The commentators agree that the destruction was by a furious, freezing wind, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi report, and that it is a lesson for the contemporaries of the Prophet Muhammad. Al-Tabari explains that the phrase 'most of them were not believers' means that most of those destroyed were not believers in God's foreknowledge. As for the closing words, 'your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful', al-Tabari explains that the Mighty is the one who takes revenge on His enemies and the Merciful is the one who shows mercy to the believers. The passage before the verse recounts Hud's exhortations to piety and obedience, his reminder of God's favours of cattle, children, gardens and springs, and his warning of a terrible day. The commentators differ on the reading of 'khuluq al-awwalin'. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it to mean the religion or custom of the ancients, while Ibn 'Ashur, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also retain the sense of the ancients' falsehood or invention. Al-Razi gives several meanings of the word rai', a high place, and of the buildings described as signposts or dovecotes, and of the masani', which according to different views are cisterns, fortresses or palaces.

This verse states that God destroyed the people of 'Ad after they denied their messenger Hud, and that this is a sign for the contemporaries of the Prophet Muhammad, most of whom were not believers. It closes by describing the Lord of the Prophet as the Mighty who takes vengeance on His enemies and the Merciful toward those who believe in Him, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain. The commentators broadly agree that the destruction came by a fierce, icy wind, as reported by Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, after the people of Hud rejected him, denied the resurrection and said that their way of life was only the custom of the ancients.

The main difference concerns the word khuluq in the phrase 'this is only the khuluq of the ancients'. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Qatada take it to mean the religion or custom of their forefathers, while Mujahid, Ibn Mas'ud and others, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, understand it as fabrication and falsehood. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that each recitation points toward one of these meanings.

The scholars also explain several terms in the passage. The word rī' is understood as a high place or road by some, and as a landmark or tower by others, while masani' is explained as water reservoirs or fortified palaces. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the phrase 'whether you admonish or not' expresses greater contempt for the admonition than a plain negative would.

The verse states that the people of Thamud denied their prophet Salih, and in doing so denied all the messengers, since their call is one and the same: the worship of God alone. Salih reminds them that he is their brother by lineage rather than by faith, urges them to fear God and obey him, and affirms that he is a trustworthy messenger who asks no reward from them, only from the Lord of the worlds. He then recalls God's favours: gardens, springs, fields and palm trees whose spathes are, according to the commentators, delicate and soft while still enclosed. They were also skilled at carving homes from the mountains. The exegetes differ on the meaning of farihin: Ibn Abbas and Abu 'Ubayda take it as skilful or proud, Mujahid as greedy, Qatada and al-Hasan as secure or comfortable, and Ibn Zayd as strong. They also differ on hadim: Ibn Abbas takes it as tender or ripe, Mujahid as crumbling when touched, and al-Dahhak and Muqatil as heaped together. Salih forbids them to obey the extravagant, the leaders of disbelief who spread corruption on earth without ever setting it right. When they ask for a sign, a she-camel emerges from the rock; Salih assigns her a share of water and them a share, and forbids harming her. They slaughter her, then regret it, but the punishment seizes them, a sign though most of them were not believers. The shared lesson is that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting the whole message.

This verse reports that Salih, the brother of the Thamud by lineage rather than faith, said to his people: will you not fear God? His question, phrased as a rebuke, urges them strongly toward piety, and he presents himself as a trustworthy messenger. The commentators agree on the plain sense: calling the people to the oneness of God and to obedience to His messenger. Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and Ibn Uthaymin note that rejecting one prophet amounts to rejecting all, since their message is one. Salih then states that he seeks no reward from them, only from the Lord of the worlds, after reminding his people of the blessings they enjoy: gardens, springs, fields, palm trees, and houses carved from the mountains.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place the Thamud in Arabia, in the region of al-Hijr between Wadi al-Qura and Syria. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the question "will you be left..." either as a reproach or as a reminder of God's favours. The commentators differ on several words: Ibn Abbas takes "hadim" to mean delicate, Mujahid to mean soft and crumbling, and al-Hasan to mean loose, while Abu Ubayda reads "fariheen" as skilful and Ibn Zayd as strong. On the phrase "among those bewitched", Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean the bewitched, while others understand it as those fed on food and drink, or as mortals of flesh like them. The scholars do not settle between these readings.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the story of Salih and his people, Thamud. Salih calls them to fear God and obey him, presenting himself as a messenger sent by God and trustworthy, and asking no reward from them except from the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Sa'di understand "trustworthy" to mean that he betrays nothing in conveying his Lord's message and sincerely wishes them well. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that Salih was known for his integrity before his mission, which strengthens the trust due to his call. The exegetes agree that all messengers preach one message, so rejecting one amounts to rejecting them all, as Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn 'Ashur point out. They also agree that the call to piety and obedience is the heart of the mission. The tafsirs spend considerable space describing the blessings this people enjoyed, gardens, springs, fields and palm trees, and the meaning of the word "hadim" about which the reports differ: delicate or ripe according to Ibn 'Abbas, crumbling to the touch according to Mujahid, pressed together according to al-Dahhak. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan record several meanings of "farihin", sometimes skilled, sometimes proud and insolent. As for "musahharin", some connect it with being bewitched, others with being sustained by food and drink, a reading supported by the people's remark that Salih is only a man like them. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Shawkani report the differing readings of "khalq" and "khuluq" in the following verse. Al-Jaza'iri draws the lesson that reminding people of God's favours leads them to gratitude and obedience.

Salih, brother of the people of Thamud, gives this command after presenting himself as a trustworthy messenger: fear God and obey me. Al-Tabari explains the fear of God here as dread of punishment for disobedience, and obedience as following his counsel and warnings, which will lead them to guidance. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri link the two terms: faith in God's oneness and obedience to His messenger. Ibn 'Ashur sees the repetition of this command as an emphasis on the core of the message shared by all prophets, and al-Sha'rawi notes that God-consciousness is paired here with obedience. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that all messengers brought one call, so rejecting one amounts to rejecting them all. Al-Biqa'i connects the command to fear the all-sovereign King with the earlier mention of his trustworthiness. Al-Sa'di stresses the gentleness of his address, reminding them of God's favours: gardens, springs and houses carved into the mountains. The next verse forbids obeying the wasteful, whom al-Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya identify as the notables and leaders of disbelief, sometimes said to be nine men who spread corruption in the land. The commentators agree that the verse asks the people to fear God and to obey the messenger in what he conveys from his Lord.

This passage from the story of Salih, peace be upon him, shows the prophet reminding his people of the blessings they enjoy, asking them to fear God and obey him, and then affirming that he seeks no wage for his mission, his reward resting with the Lord of the worlds. The commentators explain that this refusal of any payment is a sign of the messenger's sincerity and his detachment from his people's wealth. They agree that Salih was known for his trustworthiness and that his call rests on monotheism, piety and obedience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya read the mention of gardens, springs, fields and palm trees as a reminder of divine favours together with a warning that they can be taken away, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also allow that it may be a rebuke against thinking one will be left forever in such delights. On the word hadim describing the palm's spathe, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas takes it as ripe and at its full ripeness, Mujahid as crushed and falling apart at the touch, Ikrima as soft and moist, and al-Dahhak as piled one upon another, while al-Tabari settles on the sense of what is tender and moist and breaks. On the word fariheen, the readings split between the form with an alif, understood as skilled in carving the rock, and the form without it, understood as proud and insolent; al-Tabari holds both readings to be correct and well attested, and several scholars consider that they come to the same meaning.

Salih asks his people of Thamud, in rebuke, whether they think they will be left secure in what they have here below. He then lists their blessings: gardens, springs, fields and palm trees.
