The commentators read the question either as a reproach, as a reminder of God's favour, or as a warning that they should not feel safe in their possessions while disobeying. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as a reminder of blessings, while Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as a threat, asking whether they hope to keep their wealth while persisting in disobedience.

The word hadim, describing the palm blossom, has many meanings. Ibn 'Abbas explains it as ripe and mature, 'Ikrima and al-Hasan as soft and tender, Mujahid as crumbling when touched, and al-Dahhak as clustered together under the weight of fruit. Al-Tabari chooses the sense of something that breaks easily because of its tenderness and moisture, while al-Mawardi lists ten opinions and Ibn Kathir reports several.

The word fariheen has two readings. Those who read it with an alif, such as the Kufans, explain it as skilled at carving, and Ibn 'Abbas also gives the sense of shrewd. Those who read it without the alif, such as the reciters of Medina and Basra, take it as proud and insolent, a view reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Tabari holds both readings to be correct and notes that the two meanings may be combined in one word.

This passage records Salih's words to his people of Thamud: he asks whether they think they will be left secure amid the blessings around them, and reminds them of gardens, springs, fields and palm trees. The commentators explain that gardens means orchards and springs means flowing water. The palm is singled out after being included among the gardens; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read this either as honouring its superiority over other trees or as meaning that the gardens refer to other trees. The word hadim receives several meanings. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Hasan take it as ripe, soft fruit; Mujahid as fruit that crumbles at a touch; al-Dahhak as a heavy load whose clusters press against one another. Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Kathir link it to the spathe still closed and tightly packed. Al-Tabari adopts the sense of fruit made tender and moist, which is crushed by hands or by clusters rubbing together. As for fārihīn, the readers of Kufa and Ibn Amir read it with an alif, meaning skilful, while Nafi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it without, meaning arrogant and wanton. Al-Tabari holds both readings to be valid and their meanings to be close. The commentators agree that the verse reminds of God's favours and warns against heedlessness, followed by the call to fear God and obey, and the refusal to follow the corrupt chiefs.

This passage reports the words of the prophet Salih to his people Thamud: will you be left secure in what is here, in gardens, springs, crops and palm trees, and will you carve homes out of the mountains? The general meaning is a reminder of God's blessings and a warning against heedlessness toward them. As for the phrase « talʿuhā hadīm », the commentators differ. Ibn ʿAbbas and, in one report, Ibn Zayd took it as tender, ripe and moist dates in full bloom; al-Tabari, who favours this view, explains that the word means something broken by its softness and moisture. Mujahid and al-Hasan understood it as what crumbles when touched, or as what has no pit, or what is soft and loose. Al-Dahhak linked it to a heavy load that makes the fruit press against one another, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and others took it to mean slender and fine. On « fārihīn », the readings differ between the form with an alif and the form without it. The form with alif is generally explained as skilled in carving, and the form without alif as proud, insolent or exultant. Several commentators note that both readings are sound and can be combined, since they took pride in their craft while building without necessity. The passage then urges fear of God and obedience to the messenger, and warns against obeying the excessive who spread corruption without reform; most identify them as the leaders and promoters of idolatry, while some say they were the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel.

Salih reminds his people of the blessings they enjoy and asks them, in reproach, whether they think they will be left secure in what they have: gardens, springs, crops and palm trees whose spathes are heavy with fruit. The commentators differ on the meaning of “hadim”. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Atiyya take it as ripe and fully grown fruit, Ikrima and al-Hasan as soft, moist dates, Mujahid as fruit that crumbles when touched, and al-Dahhak as clusters pressed together by the weight of the harvest. Al-Tabari concludes that it means something that breaks down because of its softness and moisture. The verse then speaks of carving houses out of the mountains. Most scholars read “fariheen” as skilled and expert in the craft, as Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih and Abu Ubayda say, while Mujahid, Ibn Abbas in another report and al-Kalbi understand it as insolent pride and arrogance, and Qatada as self-admiration in their own work. Ibn Zayd takes it to mean strong. Both readings, with and without the alif, are accepted, and al-Tabari considers each correct with closely related meanings. The commentators agree that the command to fear God and obey implies not obeying the wrongdoers, the leaders who call to idolatry, and az-Zamakhshari adds that their corruption is pure, with no trace of good in it.

Salih calls his people, the Thamud, to fear God and obey him, reminding them of the blessings they enjoy: gardens, springs, crops and palm trees whose spathes are delicate and tender. The commentators differ on the word hadim describing the palm spathe. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima take it as soft or ripe dates, Mujahid as fruit that crumbles when touched, Dahhak as a heavy cluster whose fruits press against one another, and al-Hasan as fruit without a stone. Al-Tabari adopts the sense of something that yields because of its softness and moisture, while Ibn Kathir finds the early explanations close in meaning. The palm is named separately after the gardens because of its excellence, as the Arabs sometimes use the word for gardens to mean palm groves.

The word fariheen is read in two ways. The reading with an alif, followed by the Kufans, is explained by Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih as skilful in carving, and by Mujahid and Abu Ubayda as exultant or proud. The reading without an alif, followed by Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Abu Amr, is glossed by Ibn Abbas as insolent and haughty, and by Qatada as pleased with their handiwork. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct and their meanings close, and Baydawi finds the form without alif more emphatic.

Salih then tells his people not to obey the musrifun, those who exceed the limits. Ibn Abbas identifies them as polytheists, while Muqatil says they were the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel. Most commentators take them to be the leaders who spread corruption in the land without ever setting it right, and Zamakhshari observes that negating the good emphasises that their corruption is unmixed with any goodness.

In this verse, the prophet Salih, speaking to his people, tells them not to obey the command of the musrifun, those who exceed the limits in disobeying God. Most commentators identify them as the nine men of Thamud who spread corruption in the land and never reformed it, so the term refers above all to their leaders and the figures who led the people into disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi agree that this corruption was pure, with no good mixed into it, and that the negation "nor do they reform" stresses this. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil take the musrifun to be the polytheists or those who hamstrung the she-camel, and Ibn Atiyya notes that the address is to the whole people while aiming at their notables. The word "al-musahharin" has been read in different ways: Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean "the bewitched" or "the deceived", while Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi understand it as "those who eat and drink like men". Al-Tabari prefers this latter sense, supported by verses of Labid and Imru al-Qays. Others, such as Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi, link the word to the lung, meaning that Salih is merely a mortal. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that obedience is used figuratively here, either as a metaphor for carrying out a command or as attributing the commander's authority to his order. Ibn Uthaymin observes that the Qur'an speaks of the command of the musrifun rather than addressing them directly, so as to target submission to their directives.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the words of the prophet Salih to his people, Thamud. He warns them not to obey those who exceed the limits in disobeying God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that these are the nine leaders of the group, or the chiefs who call to disbelief; Muqatil, followed by al-Qurtubi, identifies them as the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel. They agree that their corruption on earth consists of sins and polytheism, and that they never do any good. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi stress that their corruption is pure, with no mixture of goodness, unlike some corrupt people who also do good. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan add that the corruption spreads across the land, since sins prevent rain. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the negation of reform reinforces the affirmation of corruption. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri explain that reform means obedience to God, and that corruption arises from grave sins. Al-Sha'rawi reads the verse as a lesson on human interference with a creation that was made in balance. The commentators agree on the general meaning and differ mainly on the identity of these people and on the exact nature of the corruption.

This verse records the reply of the people of Thamud to their prophet Salih, who had told them not to obey the extravagant men who spread corruption in the land without reforming it. They said: you are only one of the bewitched, meaning a man whose mind has been overcome by sorcery, as Mujahid and Qatada explain. Another reading, transmitted from Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi, takes the word to mean a created being who is sustained by food and drink, and some philologists connect it with the word for the lungs, so that he is simply a human with lungs who eats and drinks. Most commentators prefer the first sense, supported by the following words: you are only a man like us, so bring a sign if you are truthful, since they saw humanity as incompatible with prophethood. Ibn Kathir and others report that the sign they demanded was a she-camel brought out of a rock, and al-Qurtubi relates many accounts of the nine men who spread corruption.

The commentators agree that the people of Thamud accused Salih of madness because of his call and then demanded a miracle. They differ on the word itself: al-Tabari holds the sense of a created being who needs food, al-Mawardi lists seven meanings, including one who is deluded or intoxicated, and Ibn Atiyya judges that the context supports the sense of an ordinary mortal. Ibn Ashur explains that the second phrase reinforces the first, while al-Sha'rawi and Ibn Uthaymin consider the charge a slander, one that was made against all the prophets.

This verse records the objection of the people of Thamud to their prophet Salih, who, they said, was merely a human like themselves, and whom they challenged to bring a sign proving his truthfulness. Commentators explain the phrase "of those who are bewitched" in closely related ways: al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean people whose reason has been overcome by magic, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi take it to mean people who are sustained by food and drink, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also connect the word with the lungs. All agree that their point is that he has no distinction over them that would qualify him for prophethood. The sign they asked for was a she-camel brought out of a rock at Salih's prayer; he told them she would have her share of water on one day and they theirs on another, and warned them not to harm her. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that they slaughtered her, and the punishment came upon them. Readers differ on the form "fari-hin" or "fahi-hin", which scholars connect with skill, pride or vigour. On their regret, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that it came too late to help, while Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani understand it as fear of an imminent punishment.

This verse records Salih's reply to the people of Thamud, who had asked him for a sign proving his truthfulness: he told them that this she-camel has a share of the water and they have a set day for their own share, with neither side encroaching on the other's day. He warned them not to harm her, lest a terrible punishment of a great day seize them. The commentators agree that shirb means the portion or right to water, and that the day is called great because of the gravity of what happens in it, a phrasing that al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya consider stronger than describing the punishment itself. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the camel emerged from a rock in answer to Salih's prayer, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi describe a pregnant camel giving birth to a calf of similar size. Ibn 'Uthaymin judges the account of the rock to be an unfounded Israelite narration, while other scholars accept it. Several authors say the camel drank the whole well on her day and gave the people milk. The readings vary between the vowels i and u in shirb, and al-Zamakhshari accepts the u form. The people of Thamud eventually slaughtered the camel, and punishment struck them three days later, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya relate; their late regret did not help them once they saw the punishment.

This passage records Salih's words to his people Thamud after God had given them the she-camel as a sign. He told them that she has her share of water on a set day and they have theirs on another day, and he warned them not to harm her in any way, lest a painful punishment of a great day seize them. The commentators agree on the plain sense: a prohibition against any harm to the she-camel. Al-Tabari and Ibn Juraij say it means not to wound her, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi understand it the same way.

The word shirb (share of water) is explained by al-Zamakhshari, al-Farra and al-Nahhas as one's allotted portion of water. Al-Zamakhshari adds that on her day she drank all their water, while on their day they did not let her drink. He also records the reading with a vowel of u attributed to Ibn Abi Abla.

On the description of the day as great, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the day is called great because the punishment befalls in it, which is more forceful than describing the punishment itself. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the adjective can express praise or blame depending on context, and here it expresses blame.

Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the people eventually killed the she-camel and then regretted it when they saw the punishment. Al-Razi offers two explanations: their regret was fear of immediate punishment rather than true repentance, or it came at the moment the punishment was already visible, when repentance no longer counts. Al-Baydawi takes a similar view.

The commentators explain that Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, although their prophet Salih had warned them not to harm her, and that afterwards they regretted it, but their regret did not save them because the punishment had come. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the regret came when they saw the punishment, and Ibn Kathir describes that punishment as a great earthquake and a mighty cry. All agree that the act is ascribed to the whole people, although one man, Qidar ibn Salif, carried it out, because they approved and urged it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that this was the regret of fear of an imminent punishment rather than sincere repentance, and that repentance is not accepted when the punishment is seen. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi report that some said their regret concerned the loss of the camel's milk or of her young, a view al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir consider remote. The commentators draw the lesson that regret does not avert a punishment once it has arrived, and that this deed was an act of defiance against a sign from God. The verse also notes, in God's knowledge, that most of this people did not believe.

This verse from Surah al-Shu'ara describes the end of the people of Thamud. After they hamstrung the she-camel that Salih had given them as a sign, they regretted it when they saw the signs of punishment, and the punishment seized them as he had warned. The commentators agree that their regret was not the repentance of those who turn back to God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that it was the regret of people fearing an immediate punishment, or regret at a time when repentance was no longer accepted, namely when the punishment was seen, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi also state. Al-Qurtubi reports a weaker opinion that the regret concerned not having a child.

Most commentators take the sign to be this destruction itself, a lesson for those who reflect. Al-Tabari explains that the statement that most of them would not believe refers to what God knew in advance. Al-Baydawi adds that the denial of faith to most of them implies that had most or even a part believed, the punishment would not have befallen them, a point he relates to the Quraysh being spared thanks to the believers among them.

According to Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, the punishment took the form of a violent cry and an earthquake. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi recall that the camel had a fixed share of water and that the prohibition against harming her was a warning of a great day's punishment. Commentators differ on whether the blame falls on the one who struck the camel or on the whole people, who consented to it, a point al-Baydawi and al-Tabari both address.

The verse closes the story of Thamud with the words: 'Indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.' The commentators explain that God is the victorious Master whom none can overcome, who takes vengeance on the enemies who deny Him, and who is at the same time merciful toward those of His servants who believe in Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi connect the verse to the story of Salih and his people, who called him a liar and killed the she-camel that God had given them as a sign, so that the punishment seized them and they regretted it, but too late for repentance to help them.

Most exegetes agree that might and mercy are two inseparable attributes of God: might means irresistible power and vengeance against enemies, mercy means kindness toward believers. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i note that mentioning might removes the idea that God cannot compel people to believe, while mentioning mercy removes the idea that there is no compassion in destroying a people, since He had warned them through a messenger first. Abu al-Su'ud links the verse to the small number of believers and sees in it a hint that, had the majority believed, they would not have been seized by the punishment.

Ibn 'Ashur and others emphasize that this verset, repeated at the end of each story in the surah, serves as both a warning and a consolation for the Prophet. The pairing of might and mercy shows that God combines severity toward those who deny Him with kindness toward those who believe.

This verse states that the people of Lot denied their messenger Lot, and the commentators hold that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, since their core message is the same. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur explain that Lot was the nephew of Abraham and had settled among this people, so he is called their brother through living and dwelling with them rather than through lineage. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that he called them to fear God and obey him, declared himself a trustworthy messenger, and asked for no payment, since his reward rests with the Lord of the worlds. He then rebuked them for their practice of intercourse with men, which the commentators describe as an unprecedented sin. Opinions differ on the phrase "among the worlds": al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud read it as "among all creatures", meaning that they alone committed this act, while al-Alusi and others take it as the sons of Adam despite the great number of females among them. As for "and you leave what your Lord created for you of your spouses", al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as abandoning women, whereas al-Qurtubi takes it as leaving the female sex organ. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Qasimi, draws from it a prohibition of intercourse with a wife through the back passage, while Mujahid and others do not make it a rule, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi reads it as permission. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tha'alibi report that God rained stones upon them, and al-Qurtubi adds that the town was overturned; the commentators do not settle the exact form of the punishment.

In this verse God recounts that Lot said to his people, as a reminder and a warning: Will you not fear God? The commentators explain that this is a call to piety and to abandon the wickedness and disbelief in which they lived, which is the message of all the prophets. They agree that the verse presents a messenger counselling and warning his people, and that their rejection of him amounts to rejecting all the messengers, since their call is one and the same.

They differ, however, on the meaning of the word brother. Ibn Kathir reports that Lot was the son of Haran and nephew of Abraham, so he was of their lineage. Ibn Ashur and al-Jaza'iri hold that it is a brotherhood of residence and citizenship rather than of blood or religion, since Lot was a stranger who had settled among them; Ibn Ashur adds that he lived with them and made alliances with them. Al-Alusi says they were his in-laws, and al-Biqa'i notes that he lived among them for a long time, married among their women and had children. Ibn 'Atiyya reports, citing al-Naqqash, that the codices attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy and Hafsa omit the word brother.

All agree that the question Will you not fear God? is a rebuke that carries an appeal to fear God and to obey, and the commentators note that Lot asks them for no wage for his message, his reward resting with the Lord of the worlds.

In this verse Lot tells his people that he is a trustworthy messenger sent to them. Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi explain that his trustworthiness means he faithfully conveys what is revealed to him, adding nothing and omitting nothing, and that he asks no reward for his counsel except from the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that his message, calling people to taqwa and obedience, is the same as that of all the messengers, as al-Sha'rawi and Sayyid Qutb note. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin identify his people as those of Sodom and mention that Lot was the nephew of Abraham. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi explain that he is called their brother not by blood, since he was a stranger among them, but because he settled in their land, lived among them and allied with them.

The commentators differ mainly on the verse that follows. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the phrase the worlds as the descendants of Adam, or even all creatures that mate, while Abu Hayyan limits it to the sons of Adam. On the words what your Lord created for you of your spouses, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read min as partitive, referring to the permitted part, and see the verse as condemning both sins together. Al-Qurtubi understands the phrase as referring to the women's private parts, while Ibn Uthaymin sees a general permission to enjoy one's wife.

Lot tells his people to fear God and obey him, using the same words that earlier messengers used. Al-Tabari explains that fearing God means guarding oneself against His punishment for rejecting His messenger, and that obedience means following what he calls them to, which will guide them to the right path. Al-Biqa'i adds that obedience is the cause of their salvation, because the messenger commands only what pleases God and forbids only what displeases Him, and he stresses that God is able to destroy whomever He wills. Ibn Kathir places this call within the core message shared by all prophets, which is the worship of God alone, together with a prohibition of the sin this people had invented, namely having intercourse with men instead of women. Ibn 'Atiyya notes a point of transmission: the final ya of the word atiune is omitted in both the written text and the recitation, to match the rhythm of the verse endings, and he gives it no legal weight. Al-Sha'rawi observes that all messengers speak from one source, which explains why their words are so similar. The commentators agree that the two commands form a single call. Their differences concern emphasis: some stress the fear of punishment, others the power of God, and others the particular sin this people committed.

In this verse Lot tells his people that he asks them for no payment for his preaching, and that his reward rests only with the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari explains that he is saying he seeks no wage or recompense for his sincere counsel, for calling them to God, or for conveying God's message. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read it in the same way, and Ibn Kathir places the verse within the account of Lot's mission to the people of Sodom. The commentators agree that this disclaimer is a sign of sincerity, since a man who asks nothing from people cannot reasonably be suspected of seeking their wealth. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi quote the verse within the formula repeated for each prophet and his people, which shows that all messengers carry the same call. Al-Biqa'i draws a finer point: by limiting the reward to the Creator, Lot denies asking anything of other creatures, because God is the one who brought them into being and sustains them. Ibn 'Uthaymin sees in the verse the common principle of all messengers, namely tawhid and sincere advice. Al-Jaza'iri sums up the meaning by stating that the messenger's wage comes from God alone. The commentators do not differ on the meaning of the verse itself; their differences concern its wider context and its place within the story in the surah.

Lot rebukes his people for approaching males among the children of Adam and reproaches them for neglecting the wives that God created for them, describing them as a people who exceed the bounds. The commentators agree that the approaching refers to intercourse with men and that the reproach targets both this vice and the rejection of what is lawful. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that abandoning wives means turning from the lawful parts of women toward men's rears, with Mujahid adding women's rears as well, while al-Tabari reads it as leaving the permitted sexual parts. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the reproach does not mean abandoning women altogether, but neglecting them in their permitted place while turning elsewhere. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi offer two readings of the word 'worlds': either males excluding all other creatures, or men among humans despite the greater number of women. Al-Zamakhshari draws from the verse an argument against intercourse with a wife in a forbidden place, an inference that al-Alusi and al-Qasimi contest with counter-arguments. Ibn Sa'di and others limit themselves to a general condemnation. The narrative that follows records that the people threatened to expel Lot, that he replied he detests their deeds, and that he prayed for his family to be saved, all except his wife, who remained among those destroyed. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the act is contrary to nature, since no animal practises it.

In this verse Lot rebukes his people for approaching males among the human race while leaving aside the wives whom their Lord created for them, and he calls them a transgressing people. The commentators agree that the verse condemns intercourse with males through the posterior. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid and Ibn Juraij, explains that what God created for them means the lawful private parts of women, and he notes a reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud: what your Lord made good for you.

Scholars differ on the meaning of min in "from your wives". Most take it as explanatory. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan, reads it as partitive, meaning the permitted organ, and sees an implication that these people did the same with their own wives. Al-Zamakhshari uses this to argue that intercourse with a wife by any route other than the lawful one is forbidden, and Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi likewise present the prohibition as the prevailing view among Sunni scholars, with al-Alusi calling it a major sin. Al-Qasimi cites Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, whose view implies permissibility, but he does not accept it. Ibn Ashur adds that the phrase among the worlds signals that the act contradicts nature, since no animal species engages in it.

Finally, the words "Nay, you are a transgressing people" mark a shift from reproach to condemnation. According to Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi, the transgression may refer to this particular act, to all sins in general, or to going beyond what is naturally desired and permitted.

This verse records the response of Lot's people to their prophet, who had rebuked them for their unnatural acts. They threatened to expel him if he did not stop. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they meant banishment from among them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that they used to expel those they banished in a harsh and violent manner. The commentators agree on the nature of the sin: relations with males, while the phrase 'what your Lord created for you of your spouses' refers to lawful relations. Mujahid and Ibn al-Jawzi say this includes intercourse with women through the back passage. Ibn Ashur notes that it does not mean they abandoned women entirely, but that they avoided them at the time of the sin. On the word 'al-qali', Ibn Qutayba, al-Jawhari and Ibn al-Jawzi render it as hatred. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi stress that 'min al-qalin' is stronger than 'qali', since it indicates that he is counted among known haters of this conduct. Ibn Atiyya holds that Lot, being a stranger among them with in-law ties there, was threatened for this reason. All agree on what follows: Lot declares his abhorrence of their deeds, then asks his Lord for deliverance, which was granted to him and his family except his wife, who remained among those destroyed.

Lot, peace be upon him, answers his people, who had threatened to expel him if he did not stop rebuking them, that he is deeply hostile to their deeds. The commentators explain that the word al-qalin means those who hate. According to al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn al-Jawzi, the sin condemned is intercourse with males, and the verse rebukes these people for leaving aside what God had made lawful to them in their wives; Mujahid specifies that this refers to the front passage of women, and Ibn al-Jawzi gives the same meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note that Lot, seeing their persistence, distanced himself from them and asked God to save him and his family. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi observe that the phrase min al-qalin is stronger than qali, because it presents him as one known among those who reject this act. All agree that the woman excepted is Lot's unbelieving wife, who perished with the others. They differ on the meaning of al-ghabirin: remaining in the punishment according to al-Tabari and Qatada, or growing old according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn 'Ashur and Abu Hayyan add that the expression concerns their disobedience to Lot's message.

The commentators explain that Lot, after confronting his people about their practice of sodomy and turning away from their arguments, faced their threat to expel him from the town. He then prayed to his Lord: 'My Lord, deliver me and my family from what they do', meaning from the punishment for their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the prayer as a request for deliverance from the coming punishment, and God answered it by saving him and all his household except his wife, who was left among those destroyed.

The meaning of 'among those who remained' (al-ghabirin) is disputed. Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean those who lived on until old age; Qatada, those who remained in the torment; al-Tabari links it to her long life. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari report that a stone struck her after she left with Lot, while al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that some accounts say she never left with him at all.

All agree that Lot's wife was an unbeliever who backed her people and approved their conduct, and that the family who was saved were believers. The destruction came through the earth being overturned and a rain of stones. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan consider the phrase 'among those who hate' more emphatic than a simple 'one who hates', and Ibn 'Ashur sees a play on words. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the verb as hatred of the deed, while Ibn Juzayy reads it as expulsion. On 'what they do', Ibn Juzayy prefers the sense of being delivered from the punishment for their actions, whereas Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also allow that Lot may be asking to be preserved from similar acts.

This passage in Surat al-Shu'ara' tells how God rescued Lot and his believing household after he had called upon his Lord, having lost hope in his people, and how his wife remained among those left behind to perish. The commentators agree that "his household" means his close family and those who followed his religion, and that the exception covers his wife, who was an unbeliever, approved of her people's deed and helped them, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and others report.

The meaning of "al-ghabirin" is disputed. Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani take it to mean "those who remain", al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan connect it to remaining under the punishment, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that her remaining with those destroyed is what is meant. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the word refers to one who stays behind after others have gone, and some reports say that a stone struck her on the road, while others hold that she never left the town.

On the nature of the punishment, the commentators agree that the town was overturned and that stones rained down, but they differ on the exact mode of destruction. Al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi mention a collapse of the ground, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri stress the stones of sijjil. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the phrase "how evil was the rain of those who were warned" means that the people had been warned and did not heed. Ibn Juzayy points out that the phrase "there is surely a sign in that" is repeated at the end of each story to strengthen the lesson.

This passage describes the rescue of Lot and his household after his people threatened to expel him from their city unless he stopped denouncing them. Lot asked his Lord to save him and his family from the punishment for their deeds, and God answered his prayer. The commentators agree that Lot's wife is the one excepted from those saved. They differ on the meaning of describing her as among those who remained. Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi hold that she stayed behind in the punishment and perdition, and Qatada says she remained in God's punishment. Abu 'Ubayda adds that she remained until she grew old, a reading al-Shawkani also gives. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, however, say the phrase implies that she was destined to perish, since being left behind was not yet her state when they were saved. They also differ on where she died. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud report that a stone struck her on the road while she was leaving with Lot, while al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also mention that she never left and stayed in the town. All agree that her fate came from her disbelief, her support for her people and her approval of their acts, and that the exception covers her because of the marital bond, despite her differing faith. The commentators then describe the destruction of the rest through a sinking of the land and a rain of stones, and note that Lot's household was the only believing one in the town. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur also set out the context of the threat of expulsion.

This verse closes the story of Lot and his people in Surat al-Shu'ara'. The commentators explain that God destroyed the rest of the people after saving Lot and his believing family, except his wife, who stayed with the doomed because she approved of their deeds and helped them. Most tafsirs, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, take the destruction to be a rain of stones, and the word 'the others' to mean the people of Lot who were not saved. Al-Baghawi reports from Wahb ibn Munabbih that the rain was of brimstone and fire, while al-Qurtubi notes that some said the stones came together with a sinking of the land. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan understand the destruction to be the overturning or uprooting of the people, with the stones falling afterwards. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain that the phrase 'the rain of the warned' is a formula of blame whose object is left implicit, namely their rain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that Lot's wife perished along with those who perished. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the destruction was by stones and not by the land being turned over, since the Qur'an does not state the overturning explicitly. The commentators conclude that this punishment is a sign for those who reflect, and that most of the people did not believe, a fact known to God.

This passage from Surah al-Shu'ara describes the end of Lot's people after they had rejected their prophet and persisted in their abomination with men, neglecting the lawful wives God had created for them. They threatened to expel Lot, so he prayed to his Lord to save him and his family from the punishment of their deeds. God saved him and his household except his wife, who stayed among those who perished because she approved of their conduct and helped them. God then destroyed the rest and rained down upon them a rain of stones, a dreadful rain for those who had been warned. The commentators generally agree that the punishment was by stones, and some connect it with the overturning of the city. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the wife perished with the others; al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read the phrase about those who remained as meaning those left behind in the punishment, while Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean those who remained until old age, and Qatada as those who stayed under the punishment that descended on them. Opinions differ on the nature of the rain: according to Qatada, God rained stones on the stragglers of the people; according to Ibn Zayd, God was not content with the overturning and sent a rain of stones after it; according to Wahb ibn Munabbih, it was brimstone and fire. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the word for the warned refers to a category rather than to particular people, with the object of blame left implied: their rain. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the particle thumma marks a distance in rank, and that the word warned is a rebuke, since they were warned and did not heed.

This verse closes the account of Lot's people. It states that the destruction that came upon them, after Lot and his believing family were saved, is a clear sign of the truthfulness of the messengers, yet most people did not believe. The commentators treat it as the conclusion of the story, meant to make the listener reflect on the fate of those who denied. The same formula recurs after each story in the surah; Ibn Juzayy sees it as a reinforcement of warning and a call to the heart. On the details, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Lot prayed to God after his people threatened to expel him, and that he and his family were saved except his wife, who helped the people against him and perished with them. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi differ on the meaning of 'among those who remained': some take it as those left in the punishment, others as those who lingered into old age, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as her being destined for destruction. On how the people were destroyed, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani mention a rain of stones, while al-Qurtubi reports that Gabriel overturned the town before the stones fell. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the verse speaks only of stones, not of an overturning. All agree that Lot's household was the only believing household in the town.

This verse closes the account of Lot's people: God is the Mighty, who cannot be overcome in punishing the deniers, and the Merciful toward those who are faithful to Him. The commentators see in the repetition of this conclusion after each prophetic story in the surah a threat to the obstinate and an assurance to believers. Ibn 'Ashur reads in it a sign for the polytheists of Mecca, who passed by the ruins of those lands.

The commentators agree that Lot's people were destroyed by a rain of stones after Lot and his family were saved, except his wife, who was an unbeliever and complicit in the people's deeds. Al-Baghawi reports from Wahb ibn Munabbih that the rain was of brimstone and fire, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi speak of stones. On the destruction itself, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir extend it to those who remained in the town and to those who had left it, whereas al-Zamakhshari understands the term tadmir first as an overturning, followed by stones falling on the survivors. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that the stones were the means of destruction, and that no Qur'anic text clearly states that the town was overturned, a view others such as Ibn al-Jawzi report. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi, by contrast, describe the cities as being turned upside down after the earth gave way. Ibn Kathir stresses that most of the people did not believe, and that only those who refused faith were destroyed.

This verse states that the people of al-Aykah, a thicket of dense interlaced trees, denied their messenger Shu'ayb, and by rejecting him they rejected all the messengers, since their call is one. The commentators agree that Shu'ayb urged them to fear God and obey him, presenting himself as a trustworthy messenger who asks no wage except from the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify the people of al-Aykah with the people of Madyan, and Ibn Kathir stresses that they form a single nation. Al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Baghawi explain that Shu'ayb is not called their brother here because he was not of their lineage, whereas he is called brother when Madyan is mentioned. Qatada and Ikrima report that Shu'ayb was sent to two communities, Madyan and the people of al-Aykah, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that al-Aykah was a tribe neighbouring Madyan. On the reading, Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "Layka" without hamza, as a proper noun that is not declined, while the others read "al-Aykah". Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya reject the first reading, which Abu Hayyan defends as a transmitted, mutawatir reading. Most exegetes define al-Aykah as a thicket of dense trees, and some name the trees as dawm or muql. Shu'ayb's commands concern full measure and fair weight, not defrauding people of their rights, and not spreading corruption on earth, practices the commentators say were widespread among them.

The commentators explain that this verse opens the story of Shu'ayb with the people of al-Aykah, a thicket of dense trees. The plain meaning is that Shu'ayb asked his people whether they would not fear God and guard themselves against His punishment by giving up idolatry and sins. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that he told them he was a trustworthy messenger from God, so they should fear God and obey him. Most agree that the people of al-Aykah were the people of Madyan or close to them, and that Shu'ayb was sent to them. Several explain why the word 'their brother' is not used here: Shu'ayb was not of their lineage, unlike the people of Madyan. Ibn Kathir links this to their worship of a tree. Al-Tabari holds that the people of al-Aykah are the people of Madyan, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur consider them a separate group living near Madyan, Ibn 'Ashur finding this the more likely view. The two readings, al-Aykah and Layka, are discussed: al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan defend the common reading, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu 'Ubayd take Layka to be the name of the town. The phrase 'Will you not be God-fearing?' recurs in the call of all the messengers, a call to monotheism, obedience and refusing payment for delivering the message.

This verse presents the words of Shu'ayb to his people, the companions of the Thicket: "I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah and obey me." Commentators explain that the messenger is sent by God and is faithful to the revelation, neither adding to it nor subtracting from it, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani report. Most agree that all the prophets used this same formula, since they all command piety, obedience and sincere worship, and refuse any payment for delivering the message. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi hold that the Companions of the Thicket were a dense grove of trees, separate from the people of Madyan, and that Shu'ayb is not called their brother because he was not of their lineage. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur argue instead that they were the people of Madyan themselves, or a neighbouring tribe, with Ibn Kathir favouring a single community. On the reading "Layka", al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report that it is transmitted from Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir, while al-Zamakhshari considers it a scribal error. Several exegetes state that their punishment was the Day of the Shade, a cloud that burned them after an intense heat, though al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that some accounts of this are not authenticated.

Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, calls his people, the companions of al-Ayka, to fear God and obey him. He tells them that he is a trustworthy messenger and that he asks no reward for his mission, which is owed only by the Lord of the worlds. The commentators explain al-Ayka as a thicket of dense trees. They differ on who these people were. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Kathir hold that they were the people of Madyan themselves, while Ibn Zayd and Qatada see a desert tribe near Madyan, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn ʿAshur suggest a separate people or two communities. All note that Shuʿayb is not called their brother here, unlike in the verse about Madyan. The scholars agree that the call to piety and obedience is the common foundation of every prophetic mission. The command to give full measure and weight addressed this people's specific fraud. The word al-Jibilla is read as creation or earlier generations, with varying vowels but a broadly similar meaning. As for the punishment of the Day of the Canopy, most take it to be a cloud that shaded them after a scorching heat and then burned them, though Ibn ʿAbbas rejected some detailed narrations on this point.
brother

This verse commands the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to give full measure, not to be among those who shortchange others in measuring, to weigh with a true and straight balance, not to cheat people of their goods, and not to spread corruption on earth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy explain that this refers to shortfall in measuring and weighing and to depriving people of their rights. Ibn Kathir takes corruption here to mean highway robbery. Most commentators understand al-jibilla as the creation or the earlier peoples, while Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean creation in general. Al-Mawardi lists five meanings of al-qistas: the steelyard, iron, the standard, the balance, and justice, and notes that Mujahid and Qatada take it as a Roman word meaning justice, while Abu 'Ubayda holds it to be Arabic from al-qist. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi observe that the silence about giving more implies that whoever gives more does well, and that whoever does not is not blamed. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan discuss the readings of al-Ayka and Layka, with Abu Hayyan defending the transmitted reading. Ibn 'Ashur explains that cheating involves belittling a commodity's value to buy it cheaply. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that corruption includes killing and other acts, and cites the hadith in Ibn Majah about rain being withheld from those who cheat in measure.

God commands the people of Shu'ayb, who cheated in measure and weight, to give full measure, to weigh with a straight and just balance, not to defraud people of their goods, and not to spread corruption on earth. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the verse requires complete fairness in dealings and forbids any shortfall. On the word al-qistas, al-Hasan says it is the steelyard, al-Dahhak the standard, al-Akhfash and al-Kalbi the balance, while Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Qatada take it to mean justice, a Roman or foreign term according to them. Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Shajara regard it as an Arabic word from qist, meaning justice. Al-Tabari reads it as a balance that cheats no one, and Ibn Kathir explains that one must give as one receives. On wa la ta'thaw, Ibn al-Musayyab understands oppression after reform, Abu Malik sins, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir include highway robbery, raids and the destruction of crops. On al-jibilla al-awwalin, most read it as creation or earlier peoples. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that giving more than what is due is recommended rather than required, and the general sense is the command to be just and the prohibition of corruption.

This verse commands the people of Madyan and the Companions of the Thicket, through their prophet Shu'ayb, to give full measure and weight, to weigh with a straight and just balance, not to cheat people of their rights, and not to spread corruption on earth. The commentators explain that bakhs means diminishing people's rights, whether in measuring, weighing or other dealings. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and others add that it can also refer to the value of coins, for instance by clipping their edges.

On the word ta'thaw, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand it as highway robbery, raids, destroying crops and killing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn al-Musayyab take it as disobedience to God and injustice after the land has been set right by justice. Al-Zamakhshari links it to every kind of corruption.

The commentators agree that the command is general, covering every right of another person and every property that must not be seized or used without its owner's consent, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi say. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the repetition of the word for corrupters is not redundant but describes the state of one who corrupts deliberately, a view also taken by al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Uthaymin. Al-Tabari notes that the meaning was already explained elsewhere.

The word qistas is also discussed: al-Mawardi reports that it means the balance, the steelyard, the standard, or justice, with Mujahid and al-Sha'bi calling it a Roman word meaning justice, while Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Shajara treat it as Arabic from qist. As for al-jibilla, the commentators understand it as creation or past generations, and readings differ in vowels.

God commands the people of al-Ayka to fear Him, the One who created them and the earlier generations before them. The commentators understand that the Creator is able to destroy them as He destroyed those who came before. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy agree that al-jibilla means creation or the earlier peoples, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya note that the word also means a large crowd of people. Its vowel forms vary by reading, and al-Hasan reads it with damma.

The exegetes then report what the people said to Shu'ayb. They called him bewitched or deluded by food and drink, a mere mortal like themselves, and they took him for a liar. They asked him to make a piece of the sky fall upon them. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd explain kisafan as pieces or a side of the sky, and al-Razi says Shu'ayb left the matter to God. The punishment was the Day of the Shade, a cloud that rained fire after a scorching heat. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, quoting Ibn Abbas, warn against accounts of that day that go into detail, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi give longer narrations.

The readers differ on the name of the people of al-Ayka. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read Layka as the name of a town, while others read al-Ayka as a thicket of dense trees, which al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir accept. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy note that the text says "their brother" for Madyan but not for al-Ayka, since Shu'ayb was not of their lineage.

As for the sins, the commentators agree they were fraud in measuring and weighing. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain al-qistas as the just balance, and Mujahid links it to Greek. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir add that the prohibition covers any taking of people's rights.

The verse reports the reply of Shu'ayb's people: you are only one of those who have been bewitched, that is, a man whose reason has been disturbed by magic, and you are only a human being like us, who eats and drinks, so you have no superiority that would oblige us to follow you, and we think you are a liar in what you claim. The plain meaning is therefore an accusation of sorcery or a denial of prophethood on the ground that the prophet is human. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan pause over the waw in 'wa-ma anta': al-Zamakhshari says it shows that sorcery and humanity are each incompatible with the mission in their eyes, while others see it as added emphasis in denial. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the form without waw in the story of Thamud conveys the same sense by another route. On the phrase 'kisafan min al-sama'', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report the readings that it means a piece, a side, or a punishment from heaven; Ibn Kathir links the demand to those made by the Quraysh and by Thamud. The commentators note that Shu'ayb left knowledge of the punishment to God. As for the 'Day of the Shade', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that a scorching heat struck them, then a cloud under which they gathered rained fire, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the details of this event unverified. The differing readings of 'al-Ayka' and 'al-Layka' and of 'al-jibilla' are noted as minor linguistic variants. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi explain that Shu'ayb is not called their brother here because he was not of their lineage.

This verse records the reply of Shu'ayb's people to his call: "You are only one of the bewitched, you are merely a human like us, and we think you are among the liars." The commentators agree on this plain sense. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy regard it as a reply like that of Thamud to their prophet, while al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Uthaymin stress that it is an accusation of lying. As for the word "kisafan" in their demand, "drop upon us fragments from the sky", al-Dahhak took it to mean a side of the sky, Qatada fragments, and al-Suddi a punishment, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi explain that the particle "wa" before "you are only a human" adds a second ground of rejection, humanity, alongside being bewitched, while al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur see it as a second denial of the message. On the particle "in", the Basrans take it as a lightened form of "inna", whereas the Kufans read it as a negation, a point noted by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn Sa'di report that Shu'ayb left the matter to God, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy then came: a cloud that sheltered them after an intense heat, then rained fire. The commentators also note that the story consoles the Prophet and warns the deniers.

This verse records the reply of Shu'ayb's people when he warned them of punishment. They called him one bewitched who did not know what he was saying, a mere man like themselves with no special merit, and they considered him a liar. They then challenged him to drop pieces of the sky upon them if he was truthful. The plain sense is mockery and defiance, a demand for the punishment they dismissed, which commentators compare to words spoken by earlier peoples and by the Quraysh. Commentators differ on the word 'kisafan'. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean pieces, al-Dahhak a side of the sky, Ibn Zayd a region or a punishment, and al-Suddi a punishment, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that it may be read as singular or plural. As for 'al-sama'', some take it to mean clouds and others a canopy, the view adopted by al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani. Most point out that the answer lies in the phrase 'my Lord knows best what you do': God will repay their deeds, and the matter is not in Shu'ayb's hands. According to most, the punishment was a fierce heat followed by a cloud that sheltered them and then rained fire. Ibn 'Abbas, however, denied the reliability of the details about the day of the canopy, as Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani report. Al-Zamakhshari sees their demand as proof of their stubborn denial, and al-Razi notes that Shu'ayb left the matter to God without invoking a curse, and that God sent the punishment after they persisted in denial.

This verse reports Shu'ayb's reply to his people, who had asked him to drop a piece of the sky upon them: his Lord knows best what they do and what punishment they deserve, He will recompense them as He wills, and the punishment is not in his hands, his duty being only to deliver the message. Commentators read this as a warning to the disbelievers and a leaving of the matter to God. They differ on the meaning of the word kisf that the people demanded. Al-Dahhak took it to mean a side of the sky, Qatada pieces of it, and al-Suddi a punishment, as al-Mawardi reports. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as punishment. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, say the punishment that struck them was the Day of the Shade: a scorching heat, then a cloud they gathered under, from which fire fell and consumed them. Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, is reported to have said that whoever recounts the details of that day lies, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the truth is a punishment that God made into a shade, without further detail. Al-Razi notes the claim of the disbelievers that the delay of punishment proves Shu'ayb a liar, and Shu'ayb's response that the matter rests with God. As to the people of al-Ayka, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir describe them as dwellers of a dense thicket, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya discuss the readings ayka and layka. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that al-Ayka and Madyan were distinct peoples, an opinion others reject. For al-Sha'rawi, the sentence means that God knows who is fit to repent.

This passage tells how Shu'ayb, after calling his people to piety and to honest weights and measures, was dismissed as one bewitched and as a mere human like them. They asked him to drop a piece of the sky upon them if he was truthful. He answered that his Lord knows their deeds and will repay them, and that the punishment was not in his hands. They persisted in denying him, and the punishment of the Day of the Shade seized them. The commentators broadly agree that this was an intense heat that overwhelmed them so that neither shade nor water helped. They fled into the open desert, where a cloud gave them coolness and a breeze, but when they gathered beneath it, it rained fire upon them and they perished. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others explain that the shade itself was the cloud, and Ibn 'Abbas warned against anyone who claims detailed knowledge of that day. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud adopt this caution, while al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir himself transmit detailed accounts from several authorities. Qatada held that the people of the thicket were destroyed by the cloud and the people of Madyan by a cry, whereas others regard the two groups as one. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that they were distinct peoples. The closing formula recurs at the end of each story to fix the lesson in the heart, as az-Zamakhshari notes. Ibn 'Ashur sees the repetition of the verb of denial as a warning to the polytheists, and al-Sha'rawi observes that the punishment was harsher because it followed a hope of relief.

The verse states that the destruction of Shu'ayb's people, the companions of the Thicket, by the punishment of the Day of the Shade, is a sign for the people of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, yet most of them were not believers in God's foreknowledge. It concludes that God is the Mighty in His vengeance and the Merciful toward those of His servants who turn back to Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi read the verse as closing the seven stories of prophets that the surah recounts to console the Prophet and warn the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain the repetition of this formula at the end of each story as a way of fixing the lessons in hearts. The commentators agree that Shu'ayb's people called him a liar and asked him to drop pieces of the sky on them, and that he left the matter to God. They differ on the meaning of 'kisaf': al-Dahhak takes it as a side of the sky, Qatada as fragments, and al-Suddi as a punishment. As for the punishment of the Shade, most report that a fierce heat struck them for seven days until they took refuge under a cloud that rained fire on them. Ibn 'Abbas, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani, refused to describe the event in detail, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi judged that many of these accounts are not established. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the people of Madyan were destroyed by a cry, while those of the Thicket were destroyed by the Shade. Al-Qurtubi reports that about nine hundred people from the two groups believed in Shu'ayb.

This verse closes the account of Shu'ayb and the people of al-Aykah: the punishment they suffered on the Day of the Shade is a sign and a lesson, and most of them were not believers. The commentators explain that God is the Mighty, who prevails in His vengeance against His enemies, and the Merciful toward those who repent and turn back to Him. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that repeating this closing after each story fixes its meanings in the heart and strengthens the admonition, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that each story deserves to open and close as its companion does.

The commentators agree that these seven stories console the Prophet and warn his opponents, that the messengers' call is essentially the same, and that the people of Shu'ayb were punished for their disbelief and for cheating in measure and weight. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the punishment began with an intense heat, followed by a cloud that sheltered them and then rained fire upon them. Ibn 'Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari and al-Suyuti, reportedly said that whoever describes the details of that day has lied.

Opinions differ on the place and its name. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "Layka", which some take as the name of a town. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that al-Aykah means a dense thicket of trees, and Qatada describes trees of the doum kind. Scholars also debate whether Shu'ayb was sent both to Madyan and to the people of al-Aykah: Qatada and Ibn Zayd hold that he was, and Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes he was sent to two peoples.

The commentators explain that the pronoun in « wa innahu » refers to the Quran, and that the verse affirms it is a revelation sent down by the Lord of the worlds, not soothsaying, sorcery or poetry. Most of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, identify the Trustworthy Spirit as Gabriel, who sent it down upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ so that he would retain and understand it. Regarding the two readings of the verb « nazala », al-Tabari holds that both are well established and close in meaning: one makes Gabriel the bearer of the Quran, the other makes God the one who sent it down through him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that descent upon the heart means understanding, steadfast retention and memorisation.

The commentators explain that the clear Arabic tongue was chosen so that the people could understand the message and have no excuse. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the phrase « bi-lisanin » may be linked either to the descent or to the warning; al-Baydawi mentions that the prophets who warned in Arabic were five: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Isma'il and Muhammad. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that Ibn 'Abbas took this tongue to be that of the Quraysh.

Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir stress that the Quran is mentioned in the earlier Scriptures, and that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it. Ibn 'Atiyya considers this passage Meccan, while Muqatil holds it to be Medinan. The phrase « in the Scriptures of the ancients » is generally taken to refer to the Quran, but Muqatil, as reported by al-Baghawi, applies it to the Prophet ﷺ.

The commentators explain that this verse states the Qur'an is a revelation sent down by the Lord of the worlds, and that the Trustworthy Spirit, meaning Gabriel, brought it down upon the heart of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ so that he would be one of the warners, in clear Arabic. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi agree that the Trustworthy Spirit is Gabriel, called trustworthy because he is faithful with the revelation, and that the heart is the seat of understanding and memorisation. From the mention of the Arabic tongue they draw that the Qur'an was meant to be understood by its first audience. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan examine whether the phrase 'in a clear Arabic tongue' attaches to the descent or to the warning, and present both options. On recitation, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read 'nazala' lightly with 'al-Ruh' in the nominative, making Gabriel the subject, while Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and others read 'nazzala' with a doubled letter and 'al-Ruh' in the accusative, making God the subject. Al-Tabari considers both readings close in meaning and valid, while Abu Hatim prefers the doubled form, citing 'tanzil' in the verse before. Several commentators add that the Qur'an is mentioned in earlier scriptures, and Ibn Kathir notes that the surah denies it is the speech of soothsayers or devils. No major disagreement touches the central meaning of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms the Qur'an as a revelation sent down by the Lord of the worlds, brought by the Trustworthy Spirit, who is Gabriel, upon the heart of the Prophet so that he would be one of the warners, in clear Arabic. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Trustworthy Spirit is Gabriel, a view they present as widely accepted among the early scholars. The heart is named because it is the seat of understanding and memorization, as al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain, while al-Razi discusses at length that the heart is the seat of reason and choice. Readers differ on the vocalization of the verb and the subject: some read it lightly with the Spirit as subject, others read it intensively with the Spirit in the accusative, and al-Tabari judges both correct and close in meaning. On the Arabic tongue, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir state that it is the language of the Quraysh, so that they can understand and have no excuse. Zamakhshari adds that revelation in a foreign tongue would have led them to turn away altogether. Regarding the phrase about the earlier scriptures, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take it as a confirmation of the Qur'an's divine origin, with some seeing an allusion to the description of the Prophet in the Torah and the Gospel.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the stories of the prophets by affirming that the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit, Gabriel, upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ so that he might be a warner. Its plain meaning is that it was revealed in clear Arabic, the language of his people, so that they could have no excuse for failing to understand it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy identify the Trustworthy Spirit as Gabriel, and most attach 'in clear Arabic' to the verb 'descended'. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the heart signifies understanding and retention, and that Arabic lets the Prophet grasp the meaning at once. Al-Mawardi and al-Tabari report that the 'Arabic tongue' means that of Quraysh, according to Ibn 'Abbas, while others mention the tongue of Jurhum. Readers differ over 'nazala' lightened with 'al-rūḥ' in the nominative, or 'nazzala' doubled with 'al-rūḥa' in the accusative, and al-Tabari judges both readings equally valid. Ibn Kathir cites al-Thawri that revelation came only in Arabic. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that Arabic is the richest language for subtle meanings. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws from it that Arabic should be the language of all people.

The commentators explain that the pronoun in «and indeed it» refers to the Quran, meaning that its mention and its message are found in the scriptures of earlier prophets, although they differ on how this is to be understood. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the Quran is mentioned in earlier books such as the Torah and the Gospel, and that its coming is foretold there. Al-Mawardi reports that according to Qatada it means the mention of the Quran, according to al-Suddi the sending of the Prophet ﷺ, and according to al-Dahhak the mention of his religion and the description of his community. Muqatil holds that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ. On the «scholars of the Children of Israel», Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan mainly identify Abdullah ibn Salam and those who converted, and al-Baghawi reports that when the Meccans asked the Jews of Medina, they confirmed that the Prophet's description was in their scriptures. The commentators agree that the verse presents an argument against the polytheists: people of the Book recognise the Quran. As for «even had We sent it down upon one of the non-Arabs», al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain that the disbelievers would not have believed even if it had been recited to them in another language, while others take it as a matter of arrogance at following a non-Arab. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi report that some jurists drew from this verse a permission to recite the Quran in Persian, but al-Alusi disputes this reading.

This verse states that the Quran is mentioned in the scriptures of earlier prophets, and then answers those who ask for a sign of its truth: the scholars of the Children of Israel know it and find its description in their books. The commentators broadly agree that these scholars were primarily Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him, as reported by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Ibn Atiyya and those who cite him relate that the Meccans sent to the rabbis of Yathrib, who confirmed that the time of the Prophet was near. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that the earlier books include the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, while Ibn Kathir recalls the testimony of Jesus announcing Ahmad. On grammar, Ibn Amir reads 'takun' with a feminine verb and 'aya' in the nominative, while the majority reads 'yakun' with 'aya' as the predicate. For the next verse, al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that 'al-a'jamin' refers to those who cannot speak clearly, whether an animal or a non-Arab; al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi add that a Quran revealed in a foreign tongue would have been rejected out of arrogance. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy stress that this refusal is a hardening imposed on the wicked, and that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment. Al-Tabari also records the reading attributed to al-Farra' on 'la yu'minu', which the grammarian al-Nahhas considers mistaken.

The commentators explain that the verse means that even if the Qur'an had been revealed to a non-Arab who could not speak Arabic, and he had recited it to the Meccans, they still would not have believed, because they were stubborn and arrogant. Its purpose is to console the Prophet, peace be upon him, over the rejection of his people. The scholars differ over the word al-a'jamin. Al-Zajjaj and al-Baghawi take it as the plural of a'jam, meaning one who cannot speak clearly even if he is Arab by descent, a sense that also covers animals. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as people who are foreign to the Arabic language. Al-Hasan read al-a'jamiyyin with a double nisba yaa, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes it can be the plural of a'jam. On the phrase 'kadhalika salaknahu', al-Zamakhshari understands that denial became so firmly fixed in their hearts that it became almost innate, while al-Razi rejects a reading that would make it pure predestination without cause. Al-Tabari also cites Qatada and Ibn Zayd. Nearly all agree that refusal comes from stubbornness rather than from a lack of proof, and that they will only believe when they see the painful punishment.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of God's argument against the Meccan pagans concerning the Quran. Its meaning is that even if this inimitable speech had been sent down to a non-Arabic speaker and recited to those who turned away from the truth, they would still not have believed, because they were obstinate in rejecting what is right. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the 'scholars of the Children of Israel' with Abdullah ibn Salam and those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, a view reported from Mujahid and Qatada; al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also relate that the Meccans asked the Jews of Medina, who confirmed that the Prophet's description appeared in their scriptures. On the word 'a'jamin', al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya take it to mean those who do not speak clearly, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean a man whose language is not Arabic; al-Tabari also reports that some applied it to animals. On the phrase 'We have caused it to enter the hearts of the criminals', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand disbelief and denial, al-Zamakhshari stresses that the denial became so firmly rooted that it was like an innate disposition, and al-Razi draws from it that everything happens by God's decree and creation. The commentators agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ over his people's aversion, and that faith from them can be hoped for only when they witness the painful punishment.

The commentators explain that the verse means the criminals have been given such hardened hearts that they will not believe until they witness the painful punishment. They differ on what the pronoun in 'sallakanahu' refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take it as disbelief, denial and obstinacy being inserted into their hearts, referring back to the rejection in 'they were not believers'. This reading is attributed to al-Hasan, Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd, and to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima according to al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani. Al-Zamakhshari holds that denial has become so firmly fixed in them that it is like an innate disposition. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi draw from this that everything happens by God's decree and creation. Al-Rummani, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi take the pronoun to refer to the Qur'an itself: it entered their hearts, they understood its meanings and eloquence, yet they refused out of stubbornness. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say that 'criminals' includes the guilty of every nation, applying to the Quraysh as an example. As for 'until they see the painful punishment', most read it as a punishment that compels belief, but by then belief no longer benefits, as the story of Pharaoh shows. Al-Tabari discusses a grammatical point on whether 'they do not believe' is read in the nominative or jussive, which al-Nahhas considers an error according to the Basran grammarians. Several, including al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur, read 'suddenly' as a warning of sudden punishment, whether death, the Last Day, or the defeat at Badr.

The commentators explain that the verse states that the Quraysh will not believe in the Qur'an until they witness the painful punishment, meaning that their obstinacy is so fixed in their hearts that only the punishment itself will bring them to belief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand this punishment as the torment of this world, of death, or of the Day of Resurrection, depending on the reading. They also agree that faith at the moment the punishment is seen brings no benefit. Ibn Kathir reports that Pharaoh believed only when drowning, and cites other verses to the same effect. Nearly all of them take the pronoun in 'salaknahu' to refer to denial, disbelief or hardness of heart, which God caused to enter the hearts of the guilty. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that attributing this to God signifies how firmly rooted this denial became, and al-Razi presents the arguments on each side of the question of predestination without choosing between them. Al-Tabari holds that 'la yu'minun' is in the nominative, while al-Nahhas considers the jussive form an error according to the Basran grammarians.

Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect the verse to the warning against the polytheists who demanded the punishment, and to the idea that God grants them respite before seizing them suddenly. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the phrase refers to the guilty of every nation, with Quraysh as an example, and that it was fulfilled at Badr. Ibn 'Ashur finds that the punishment may refer both to the afterlife and to the sword at Badr. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi add that faith at that point is the faith of despair, which brings no benefit.

This verse says that those who reject the Quran will not believe until they see the painful punishment, and that it will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware. When it arrives they will wish to be given respite so they can repent and believe. The commentators agree that the 'criminals' are the polytheists and that faith no longer benefits once the punishment is seen. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the wish as a cry of distress at that moment, and Ibn Kathir cites Pharaoh as an example. Al-Baghawi, quoting Muqatil, notes that the Meccans had been asking when the punishment would come. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that the verse was fulfilled at Badr, a view other scholars do not share. Al-Hasan read the verb in the feminine and took it to mean the Hour. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the 'fa' here marks an escalation in severity rather than an immediate sequence, a position taken up by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a real succession. Most commentators link the verse to what follows, where God rebukes the Quraysh for hastening the punishment and shows that long enjoyment of worldly comforts will not help when it comes. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi add that God never destroys a community without first sending it a warner.

This verse describes the disbelievers when punishment seizes them suddenly, while they are unaware of it. They then cry out in regret: will we be given a respite?
