The commentators explain that this is a vain wish, the question carrying the sense of longing. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as a request for delay in order to turn back from disbelief and believe. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the particle fa indicates a ranking of severity rather than a sequence in time: what is hardest for them is to ask for respite after seeing punishment arrive. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi add that this regret recurs for every wrongdoer who sees his punishment. Ibn Ashur suggests the punishment may be death or the sword at Badr, or the punishment of the Hereafter, while al-Biqa'i and al-Nasafi see the request as a wish to be spared even for a moment. The commentators agree that this request will not be granted. The next verse rebukes the Quraysh for hastening punishment, and the following verses note that enjoyment of worldly life will not protect them, and that God never destroyed a town without sending a warner. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir confirm that punishment comes only after warning. The apparent meaning is therefore the belated regret of those who rejected the truth.

This verse asks the disbelievers in a tone of rebuke and disapproval whether they are seeking to hasten Our punishment. The commentators explain that the polytheists of Mecca mocked the Prophet and demanded that the punishment be brought at once, saying: rain stones upon us from heaven, or bring us what you threaten. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the verse as addressed to the Quraysh, while al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi connect the demand to the moment when the Prophet warned them. All agree on the core meaning: this haste springs from arrogance, mockery and trust in a long respite. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan link the question to the preceding verses, where the wicked ask for a delay once punishment strikes, or read it as an astonished question standing on its own. The verses that follow, about the long enjoyment of worldly goods that profits nothing against punishment, are read by Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn Sa'di as the natural continuation of this reproach. Ibn Sa'di stresses that what matters is not whether punishment comes early or late, but guarding against deserving it. The scholars thus share one lesson: the respite granted is no proof of safety, and eagerness to demand punishment reveals a disordered mind.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet: "Have you considered: if We let them enjoy comforts for years...", meaning, tell me what would happen if We prolonged their lives and granted them the pleasures of this world for many years, and then the promised punishment came upon them. It closes a passage in which the disbelievers mocked and demanded the punishment hastily, and asked for respite once it arrived. The commentators agree on the central point: a long period of enjoyment neither averts the punishment nor lightens it. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi all read it this way. Ibn Kathir cites a saying attributed to 'Umar that it is as if one had never spent a restful night once one attains one's aim. As to the word "years", 'Ikrima took it to mean the age of this world, while Shurayk ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nakha'i took it to be forty years; most exegetes, including al-Sam'ani, say no precise number is intended, only many years. Al-Sam'ani defines enjoyment as living in what is pleasant and desired. The verb is read in another form by some reciters. On the addressees, al-Qurtubi reports that according to al-Dahhak they are the people of Mecca, while Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy give the sense as general. Ibn al-Qayyim cites the verse to illustrate the shortness of hope, and Ibn Kathir relates a hadith about the disbeliever plunged into the Fire who recalls no good at all. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shawkani see in it a warning against feeling secure.

The commentators explain that this verse continues the address to those who will not believe in the Qur'an until they see the painful punishment. When it comes upon them suddenly while they are unaware, they ask for a respite. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the punishment to mean the punishment of this world or the punishment at death, when the disbeliever wishes to return, whereas al-Razi sees their plea as a gasp for relief once escape has become impossible. As for the words "Have you considered: if We let them enjoy for years", Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that a long period of enjoyment does not protect them once the punishment arrives. Ikrima says that "years" may mean the lifespan of the world. All agree that this enjoyment will profit them nothing. They also note that God never destroyed a town without sending warners to it, which the word "a reminder" expresses. The grammatical analysis of this word differs: al-Kisa'i takes it as a circumstantial accusative, al-Zajjaj as an absolute object, al-Zamakhshari as an object of purpose, and Ibn 'Atiyya as the predicate of an implied subject. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi note that the passage follows the rebuke of those who hastily demand the punishment. The commentators present these opinions without choosing between them.

This verse states that when the promised punishment comes upon the disbelievers, the years of comfort they enjoyed will not help them at all. Al-Tabari explains that the respite and enjoyment neither protected them nor lightened their punishment, and only increased their sins. Ibn Kathir adds that such comfort will come to seem as though it never existed, and he cites a hadith about the most fortunate of people in the Fire. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that a long life is of no benefit once the punishment arrives.

The commentators agree on the central lesson: respite does not mean escape, because what is coming is near, as Abu Hayyan says. Several identify the years mentioned with the lifespan of this world, following Ikrima, while al-Dahhak takes the people in question to be the inhabitants of Mecca. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi present the verse as a warning, and it is reported that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz recited it every morning.

Opinions differ on how the verse connects to its context. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi offer several ways of linking it to the preceding verses, and Abu Hayyan criticises one of them. There is also disagreement over the particle ma: most read it as an interrogative with the force of a negation, while others take it as a plain negation. The following verse, which states that no town was destroyed without a warner sent to it first, is read by several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di, as an affirmation of God's justice.

The commentators explain that God never destroyed a town without first sending messengers to warn its people, so that the proof was established against them and the warning served as a reminder. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di agree that the phrase 'and We were never unjust' means that God does not punish a people before warning them, so destruction after the warning is not an injustice. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir identify the warners as the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari reads 'a reminder' (dhikra) as an accusative noun meaning a reminder, and also as an object of purpose or a predicate of a hidden subject, and he gives special weight to the idea that such destructions serve as a lesson for others. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan reject this last reading on grammatical grounds, arguing that a purpose complement cannot depend on the verb placed before 'illa'. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss several parsings and places to pause. The verse is linked in the commentaries to the unbelievers who asked for the punishment to come quickly; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the comforts they enjoyed in this life will not help them when the punishment arrives. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also reject the claim of the polytheists that the devils brought down the Qur'an, since they are kept away from hearing the heavens.

The commentators explain that God never destroyed a town without first sending it warners, so that the message would be a reminder and a warning to its people, and that God, in punishing them after the warning, was not unjust. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj identify the warners as the messengers, and Ibn Kathir stresses that God never punishes a nation before establishing proof against it.

The grammar of the word "dhikra" is discussed. Al-Zajjaj and others take it as an accusative verbal noun meaning "reminder", al-Kisa'i takes it as a circumstantial accusative, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see it as an object of purpose, so that the destruction serves as a lesson for others. Others, including Ibn 'Atiyya, read it as the predicate of an implied subject meaning "this is a reminder". Abu Hayyan objects to the reading in which it depends on "ahlakna", since what precedes "illa" does not govern what follows it, and he therefore considers that reading weak.

The commentators agree that "wa ma kunna zalimin" affirms God's freedom from injustice, meaning that He would not destroy people who were innocent before being warned. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws the lesson that a religious duty does not bind a person before knowledge of it reaches him.

The next verse, according to most exegetes, answers the polytheists' claim that demons inspire the Qur'an to Muhammad. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, and that the demons are kept away from eavesdropping by meteors. Al-Tabari judges al-Hasan's reading "al-shayatun" to be a solecism.

This verse denies that the Quran was brought down by devils, answering the accusation of the Meccan polytheists that Muhammad was a soothsayer inspired by demons. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that the devils neither could nor should bring it down, because they are cut off from listening to the heavens and are pelted with meteors. Al-Mawardi gives three senses of being kept away: from hearing the Quran, from understanding it, or from acting on it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur explain that devilish souls are dark and corrupt by nature and cannot receive what descends from the angelic realm, while Ibn Atiyya links the screening to the earlier practice of devils sitting to eavesdrop. Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Muqatil, reports that this is the occasion of revelation, the Quraysh having claimed that devils fed the Quran to Muhammad. Ibn Kathir also notes that the Quran was protected during its descent. The reading of al-Hasan, «ash-shayatun» with a waw, is judged faulty by al-Farra', al-Nahhas and Abu Hayyan, though some grammarians, including al-Mu'arrij, offer a possible justification from the root. Ibn Ashur notes that divination rests on the fabrications of soothsayers, which the Quran cannot resemble. Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on the following verses, connects the passage to the duty to warn the closest kin.

This verse belongs to the Qur'an's answer to the pagans' claim that the revelation is of the same kind as what devils whisper to soothsayers. The commentators explain 'and it is not fitting for them' as meaning that it is not proper or suitable for them, and 'nor are they able to' as meaning that they simply cannot do it. Ibn Kathir understands it as a difference in nature: the devils seek corruption and misguidance, while the Qur'an enjoins good, forbids evil, and is light and guidance, so the two are utterly incompatible. Al-Tabari adds that they cannot reach the place in the heavens where the message is received. The verse then gives the reason: they are kept away from hearing from above. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi see this as a direct refutation of the charge of soothsaying. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud add that the Qur'an contains unseen truths that only angels can convey, and that the souls of devils are impure by nature. Ibn 'Ashur holds that soothsayers merely voice their own thoughts and that shooting stars ended the practice with Islam. As for the reading attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri, 'al-shayatun' with a waw, most grammarians and readers reject it as an error, including Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas, while a few try to justify it by analogy with place names such as Yabrin and Filastin.

The commentators explain that this verse (26:212) answers the claim of the polytheists that the Qur'an is of the same kind as what devils convey to soothsayers. They state that the devils neither can bring this revelation down nor are they fit for it, because they are kept away from listening to the angels in heaven. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say that shooting stars keep them away, and Ibn Kathir sees this as a mercy from God and a protection of the Law. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Razi add that the impossibility also stems from the nature of devils, whose souls are dark and evil and cannot receive the hidden truths that come only from the angels. Al-Mawardi offers three readings: being kept from hearing the Qur'an, from understanding it, or from acting upon it. Al-Sam'ani takes the expression to mean being veiled. Regarding the reading attributed to al-Hasan, "al-shayatun" with a waw, al-Farra' calls it an error, al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi reject it, while al-Mu'arrij and Abu Hayyan offer a possible derivation for it. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the Arab belief that devils eavesdrop on the higher world, a practice the Qur'an's revelation has ended. Ibn Sa'di stresses that God punishes only after warning, and Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that accountability presupposes knowledge.

This verse forbids calling upon any other god alongside Allah. Although addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, who could never commit this act, commentators agree the warning is meant for all people. Ibn 'Abbas explains it as a warning to others: even you, were you to take another god, would be punished by Me. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read it as an exhortation to deepen sincerity and a gentle lesson for all believers, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that the address is directed at leaders while intending their followers. Ibn 'Ashur holds that it addresses anyone who hears the words. The next verse orders the Prophet to warn his closest kin. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that he began with the descendants of 'Abd al-Muttalib, calling on Safiyya and Fatima and telling them he could not help them before Allah. Ibn Kathir, however, judges the longer account narrated from 'Ali about the feast for the clan to be weak because of one of its transmitters. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Atiyya argue the warning remains general, with kinship singled out because relatives are more likely to listen and more readily tolerated. The third verse commands lowering one's wing, meaning gentleness, toward the believers who follow him; Ibn Zayd explains this as gentleness of speech. If the kinsmen disobey, he should declare himself free of what they do, which most understand as disavowing their polytheism, though Abu Hayyan says it does not mean disowning the followers. Finally, the phrase about the one who sees you when you stand has several readings: prayer alone, according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada; the Prophet's movements in congregational prayer with the believers; or, according to Mujahid, his ability to see behind him.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to warn his closest kin of his tribe, meaning his nearest relatives. The commentators explain that the warning concerns Allah's punishment for associating partners with Him and for sins, and that only faith can save them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the Prophet carried out the command: he gathered the Quraysh, then the descendants of 'Abd al-Muttalib and Hashim, called his relatives by name and told them he could do nothing to protect them from Allah. Most note that the warning was first directed at the family before being extended to all, and al-Zamakhshari gives the reason: a relative might be suspected of partiality, so the Prophet wanted to show that he favoured no one. The word 'ashira is taken by most to mean the nearest kin within the tribe, but opinions differ on the group meant: the Quraysh according to some, Banu 'Abd Manaf according to others, and Banu Hashim according to still others. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate well-known accounts of the Prophet climbing al-Safa and of the meal he gave the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, though Ibn Kathir judges some of the chains of transmission weak. The instruction to lower the wing toward the believers is read by all as gentleness and humility. For the phrase, if they disobey you, say: I am free of what you do, most take it as a disavowal of association with God and its adherents. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this passage was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while the other commentators do not mention this.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to lower his wing, that is, to be gentle and humble toward the believers who follow him. The image comes from a bird lowering its wings when it descends, a sign of tenderness and humility. The commentators agree that the verse calls for gentleness, kind treatment and consideration toward the believers, and that it addresses believers of his own kin as well as others. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir connect it to the preceding verse, which ordered him to warn his closest relatives: after the firmness of that warning, gentleness toward the faithful. Al-Tabari reports, through Ibn Juraij, that the Muslims were distressed that the Prophet began with his own family, and that this verse was revealed to reassure them. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate that he obeyed by gathering the Quraysh and the Banu Hashim. On the meaning of "believers", al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it to mean those who profess faith with their tongues or are close to faith, while al-Razi holds that many followed him out of kinship rather than conviction. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that whoever disobeys afterward is to be disowned, a point Ibn Kathir links to rejecting idolatry and disobedience. The commentators present these views without judging between them.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ that if his closest kin disobey him and persist in idolatry, he should openly declare his disavowal of their deeds, and place his trust in God, the Mighty, the Merciful. Commentators agree that the plain meaning concerns rejecting polytheism and disobedience. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su'ud take it as a call to renounce idol worship. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the verse to believers who follow the Prophet: if they disobey him, he must disassociate himself from them and their actions. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan see a temporary truce abrogated by the verse of the sword, and Ibn Zayd also speaks of abrogation. Ibn 'Ashur holds that this disavowal does not prevent maintaining family ties and continuing to advise one's relatives. Al-Alusi mentions the view that the disavowal targets opposition to Islamic rulings rather than the whole people. For the following verse, most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy, explain 'who sees you when you stand' as seeing you rise for prayer, and 'your movements among those who prostrate' as your posture in prayer with the believers. Mujahid understands that the Prophet could see behind him, while al-Hasan takes it as his movements among his companions. Al-Razi offers several readings, including the Prophet's night prayer.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to put his trust in the Almighty, who overcomes His enemies, and the Merciful to His believers, and to entrust his affair to Him, who will suffice him against the harm of those among his people who disobey him. The commentators explain 'who sees you when you stand' in different ways: he sees you when you stand for prayer, says Ibn Abbas; wherever you are, says Mujahid; when you rise from your bed or your seat, says al-Dahhak; in all your states, says Qatada. As for 'and your movement among those who prostrate', views differ. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Ata and most exegetes take it to mean his movements in prayer, standing, bowing and prostrating, and al-Tabari prefers this view as the most apparent meaning. Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi understand it as his praying with the congregation, while Mujahid says he could see those behind him as well as those in front, a view supported by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir through the hadith 'I see you from behind my back'. Others, such as Ibn Abbas and Ata, read it as the Prophet's passage from the loins of prophets until his birth, al-Hasan as his coming and going among his companions, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as his conduct like that of the prophets before him. The readings also differ between 'fa-tawakkal' with fa, read in Medina and Syria, and 'wa-tawakkal' with wa, read by the rest. The verse ends by stating that God is the All-Hearing, who hears what he says and knows what he intends and does.

In this verse God commands His Messenger ﷺ to put his trust in Him alone, the Mighty who overcomes His enemies and the Merciful to His allies, and then describes Him as the One who sees him when he stands up. The commentators agree that "when you stand" refers to standing for prayer, though Mujahid takes it to mean standing anywhere, al-Dahhak standing up from one's bed, Qatada all his states, and al-Hasan being alone. On the phrase "and your movement among those who prostrate", opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and most exegetes take it to mean that He sees your movements in prayer: standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting. Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand the prostrators as those praying, meaning He sees you praying with the congregation. Mujahid explains that he sees the turning of his gaze toward those behind him, as he sees those in front. Ibn Kathir and others report that Ibn Abbas and Ata understood it as God's moving him through the loins of prophets until he was born, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr took the prostrators to be the prophets, with the movement meaning his conduct of affairs as the prophets did before him. Tabari judges that the most apparent meaning is His seeing your movement with the believers in prayer. Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite further readings linked to preaching and fighting the polytheists. The verse ends by affirming that He is the Hearer of your recitation and your supplication, and the Knower of your deeds and of those who pray with you.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the command given to the Prophet ﷺ to put his trust in God, the Mighty, the Merciful, and that God sees him when he stands to pray and sees his movements. On the phrase "and your turning about among those who prostrate," the views differ widely. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, along with al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean his movements in prayer with the worshippers, standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting; al-Tabari adopts this as the most apparent sense. Mujahid holds that the Prophet could see behind him as clearly as in front, citing a sound hadith. In another report Ibn 'Abbas explains it as the Prophet's passage from one prophet's lineage to another until he was born, a view repeated by al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, who also mentions other readings. Others understand it as his movements among the believers, or that the prostrators are earlier prophets. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as the Prophet's attention to his companions during night prayer, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers that meaning out of place here. Al-Razi and al-Alusi bring the verse into the debate on the faith of the Prophet's parents; Ibn Kathir firmly rejects that reading, and al-Alusi says he does not use the verse as proof of it. The commentators conclude that God hears words and knows deeds, which is the basis for trusting Him.

In these verses God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to disown those of his close kin who disobey him, especially those who worship idols, to put his trust in his Lord, the Mighty and Merciful, and to be assured that God sees him when he stands to pray and sees his movements among those who prostrate. The closing phrase, 'He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing,' means that God hears what the Prophet says and knows what he intends and does. The commentators agree that 'standing' generally refers to prayer and that 'those who prostrate' are those who pray. They differ, however, on the meaning of 'your movements among those who prostrate.' Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', Qatada and Muqatil take it to mean his movements standing, bowing and prostrating together with the congregation in prayer, which al-Tabari adopts as the most apparent sense. Mujahid holds that he could see behind him as well as in front, relying on an authentic hadith. Al-Hasan understands it as his comings and goings among his companions, Sa'id ibn Jubayr as his conduct in the manner of earlier prophets, and Ibn 'Abbas, in another report, as the transfer of the Prophet through the loins of prophets until his birth. Al-Razi rejects some of these readings on doctrinal grounds, while Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin mention the lesson on congregational prayer. Many commentators, such as al-Sam'ani, consider the final phrase to be plain in meaning. The commentators agree on the overall sense of comfort and protection the passage gives to the Prophet.

This verse states that the devils descend only upon those who resemble them: lying, sinful people, namely soothsayers. The commentators read it as a reply to the pagans who claimed that a devil inspired the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi mostly identify the 'great liar, sinner' as soothsayers, while Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean any liar among men. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report that the devils once overheard the angels, then passed fragments to their human allies, to whom they added many lies, citing the hadith of 'A'isha about the snatched word and the hundred lies added to it. On 'they cast the hearing', some take the devils as subject, others the soothsayers; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the soothsayers, Ibn Kathir noting that the devils heard the angels. As for 'most of them are liars', al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that few soothsayers speak truly about what they attribute to the jinn, while others take the devils themselves as the referent. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi connect the passage to the argument that the Prophet's conduct, unlike that of soothsayers, refutes the accusation. The surah then turns to poets, followed by the misguided. Commentators differ on who these misguided are: narrators, foolish people, or devils. They agree that the poet wanders through every kind of speech and says what he does not do, but they exclude believing poets who defend Islam, such as Hassan, Ibn Rawaha and Ka'b ibn Malik according to the reports, despite the question of a Meccan surah's occasion of revelation. Al-Jaza'iri concludes that these verses reject the claim that the Prophet was a soothsayer or a poet.

This verse says that the devils descend only upon one who is much given to lying and sin, namely soothsayers and false prophets, with some commentators naming Musaylima, Tulayha and Satih. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that it answers those who claimed the Prophet ﷺ received the Qur'an from the jinn, since his truthfulness and righteousness cannot match such an inspiration. On the phrase 'they cast the hearing', the commentators differ. Mujahid, Qatada and, in one narration, Ibn 'Abbas explain that the devils eavesdrop on the angels and pass what they hear to the soothsayers, while others, including al-Zamakhshari, take the pronoun as referring to the soothsayers who relay what they heard. The phrase 'most of them are liars' is read by some as referring to the devils and by others to the soothsayers. Al-Zamakhshari notes that 'affak' means one who greatly multiplies falsehood, not one who speaks only falsehood, so that only a few of them tell the truth. The hadith of Aisha, in which the jinn snatches a true word and adds more than a hundred lies to it, is cited by most. Al-Alusi and others debate whether this eavesdropping ended with the mission of the Prophet, some holding that it ceased entirely, others that it continued in other forms.

These verses state that demons descend only upon those who resemble them, namely liars and sinners such as soothsayers, and that the Prophet ﷺ is far removed from such a state. According to the commentators, the demons pass on to their human allies what they overhear, and most of what is passed on is false. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, identify the 'much-lying sinner' with soothsayers, citing the hadith from Aisha that a true word is snatched by a jinn who whispers it into his ally's ear and then adds more than a hundred lies. Al-Tabari also reports this identification from Qatada and Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow that the pronoun in 'they cast the hearing' may refer either to the liars or to the demons, and they describe several ways of understanding what is conveyed. Ibn 'Atiyya leans toward the pronoun referring to the soothsayers. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn say that the stealing of hearing took place before the mission and that the demons were afterwards barred from the heavens. Al-Alusi lists several possibilities about the timing and manner of this eavesdropping without settling on one. The following verses are linked by the commentators to the description of poets: the misguided follow them, they wander through every valley of speech, and they say what they do not do. Ibn Kathir and others exclude believing poets who answered the polytheists' satire. Several authors cite hadiths both criticising and permitting poetry, and the case of al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, where the verse 'they say what they do not do' was used to avert a penalty, is reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi.

This verse states that poets are followed by the misguided. The commentators differ on who these followers are: Ibn Abbas, in one transmission, and al-Dahhak identify them as reciters of poetry or fools who side with the poet, Mujahid and Qatada as the devils, while Ibn Zayd and Ikrima name the polytheists or the rabble. Al-Tabari holds that the verse covers every category of the misguided, among both humans and jinn. As for 'they wander in every valley', Ibn Abbas explains it as engaging in every vain discourse, Mujahid as the variety of poetic genres, and Qatada as praising some falsely and blaming others unjustly; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the valley as an image for the topics of verse. The phrase 'they say what they do not do' is explained by Ibn Abbas as meaning that most of their speech is false, and some jurists relied on it to avert the legal penalty from a poet who had confessed a fault in his verses, as in the account of Umar and al-Nu'man ibn Adi. There is consensus that the exception 'except those who believe' refers to Muslim poets such as Hassan ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Rawaha and Ka'b ibn Malik. They differ on 'and remember Allah often': some take it as referring to their speech, others to their poetry. 'And who defend themselves after being wronged' refers to answering the polytheists' satires against the Prophet and the believers. The verse closes with a warning to the wrongdoers that they will learn what final return awaits them. Al-Zamakhshari takes the restriction from the word order, while Ibn Ashur holds that the verse blames the poets and their followers without making poetry forbidden in itself, the judgment resting on its content and its author.

This verse describes poets as men who wander from one theme to another "in every valley", without a fixed aim, like one who roams aimlessly, and who say what they do not do. The commentators agree that it refers to the pagan poets who mocked the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims, and to those who follow them, described as the misguided. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report several meanings of "the misguided": demons, unbelievers, fools, or the reciters of poetry. As for the "valley", Ibn Abbas takes it to mean every kind of idle talk, Mujahid every kind of discourse, and Qatada praising some people falsely while insulting others falsely. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that wandering means straying from the right path, while others understand it as excess in praise or blame. On "they say what they do not do", most read it as lying, such as boasting of generosity or courage one does not possess. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate that ‘Umar dismissed al-Nu'man ibn ‘Adi from his post without imposing the prescribed punishment, the verse having been cited in his defence, and the case of Farazdaq before Sulayman ibn ‘Abd al-Malik is also mentioned. The following verses except believing poets who do good, remember God often and defend themselves after being wronged; Ibn Abbas and most commentators apply this to Hassan ibn Thabit, Ibn Rawaha and Ka'b ibn Malik, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur extend the rule to anyone of similar character. The commentators stress that poetry is not condemned in itself, but only what it contains of falsehood.

This passage describes the blamed poets as men driven by desire and falsehood, followed by the misguided. The commentators differ on who is meant: the poets may be the poets of the polytheists, and the "misguided" may be transmitters of poetry, foolish people, devils, or the misguided among jinn and men. The phrase "wandering in every valley" means, according to Qatada, that they praise some and blame others without basis, and according to Ibn Abbas, that they plunge into every kind of idle talk. "And that they say what they do not do" means that most of their words are lies or boasts that are never acted upon. Some scholars cited this verse to dismiss a legal punishment against a poet who confessed in his verses to drinking wine, as reported in the story of al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi. The commentators agree that the exception covers believing poets who did good, remembered God often and answered those who attacked them, such as Hassan ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Rawaha and Ka'b ibn Malik. Al-Razi and most others see the verse as condemning the way of the idolatrous poets, set against the Prophet's ﷺ conduct, while some extend the censure to disbelievers in general. Most note that poetry is not blamed in itself, only when it contains falsehood and insult, supported by the saying: "Indeed, some poetry contains wisdom."

This verse says that the poets followed by the misguided wander through every valley of speech, praising and blaming without truth, and saying what they do not do. God then excepts those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember God often and defend themselves after being wronged, and warns the wrongdoers that they will learn to what final return they are going. The commentators agree that the exception covers the Muslim poets who defended the Prophet ﷺ against the satires of the pagans, such as Hassan ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Rawaha and Ka'b ibn Malik; Ibn Kathir adds that it also includes any poet who repented of attacking Islam. On the meaning of 'the misguided', Ibn Abbas takes them to be the reciters of poetry, Mujahid and Qatada the devils, al-Dahhak the foolish, and Ibn Zayd the polytheists; al-Tabari holds that all these groups are meant. On 'remembering God much', Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand it as speech, Ibn Zayd as poetry, and Ibn Kathir accepts both. 'Defending themselves' is generally taken to mean answering satire with satire against those who attacked the believers. Al-Zamakhshari holds that poetry is a branch of speech, good when its content is good and bad when it is bad. Most explain 'wronged' as idolatry and insult to the Prophet, though al-Zamakhshari considers this too narrow. A minority reading, 'munfalat', meaning escape, is also recorded.
